INTEREST RATES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the announcement yesterday of the increase in the Bank of Canada rediscount rate to an unprecedented 4.9 per cent, an increase of more than 300 per cent in eight months, and the consequent further disturbing announcement of the increase in the prime lending rate of the chartered banks which raises for Canadians the spectre of higher interest rates generally, as has already been made apparent by other announcements by finance companies, and the need for immediate action by government to roll back interest rates and remove this threat to economic recovery.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INTEREST RATES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Assiniboia has moved under standing order 26 for leave to present a motion for the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. I note that subsection 6 of the rule provides:
The right to move the adjournment of the house for the above purposes is subject to the following restrictions:
(c) the motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session:
Although there has been no separate debate on this specific subject, we have just completed the eight-day budget debate in which this matter was raised and when there was full opportunity to discuss a financial issue of this kind. It seems to me that as the problem which the hon. member desires to debate, the question of high interest rates, is one that has not risen suddenly but has been a phenomenon of the past few months, and a widespread phenomenon, there has been ample opportunity for discussion during the course of the budget debate. My disposition
would be to say that this is not a matter for which we should interrupt our proceedings at the present time.

subtopic: INTEREST RATES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
So far as your intimation is concerned that this would be out of order because the matter had been discussed previously, I would suggest that is something that cannot be applied to this proceeding. It is a well known rule that if the house makes a decision on a given matter, it is impossible then to raise the same matter again in the same session. However, the mere discussion of any particular subject does not rule out its subsequent discussion at a later time during the session.
So far as the statement that this phenomenon has been going on for a number of months is concerned, of course that is a statement of fact. But it would seem to me that it is particularly urgent at this time because certain finance companies, certain mortgage companies, are announcing that they will take steps now, in the light of a number of previous rises in interest rates, to increase the interest charges they now make. We feel it is extremely urgent at this time to deal with this question because the rate is the highest in history and because it is now affecting interest rates to the ordinary Canadian citizen all across our country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INTEREST RATES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one further point I should like to draw to your attention, and it is this. Last night in announcing the business of the house for next week I indicated that we would be discussing the budget resolutions, so there will be ample opportunity when these resolutions come up for a discussion of this nature to take place.
Surely this rule was never intended to enable an hon. member of the house to get up whenever there happened to be a change -for example in the interest rate-and move to adjourn the house. There may be many other similar types of changes that are made from time to time in the course of the administration of public affairs and, as Your Honour said, there have been other changes in the rates. The rates will probably be lowered one of these days, and of course we will not see my hon. friend jumping up to move to adjourn the house on that occasion bceause there would be no political hay to be made in such an event.

Finance
I suggest that if it is to be the practice in this house that whenever a change is made motions are moved to adjourn the house, the business of parliament would be made simply impossible. This would seem to be a matter of propaganda, and I suggest the motion should not be allowed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: INTEREST RATES
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly disagree with the leader of the house that this is a matter of propaganda. On the contrary, it is a very serious matter that will affect the rights of everyone in this country. As the hon. member for Assiniboia has just said, this is an occasion on which the interest rate has reached the highest point ever in the history of this country, and that surely is a serious matter.
I want to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the answer given by the leader of the house does not at all meet the position which has been laid before you. It is not a fact that the budget resolutions will dispose of this matter. It is true that the house leader announced the discussion of the budget resolutions, but as the business of the house is proceeded with the house knows full well that the budget resolutions may not be reached until Wednesday or Thursday or even until the end of next week. And then again, I might ask, when the budget resolutions are reached, which of them deals with the matter that is now before Your Honour for discussion?

speechtext: None.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:

This matter is not only of tremendous importance to the house but it is of equal importance to the people of this country. It is a matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) prior to the orders of the day yesterday, and certainly it should receive the proper discussion to which a matter of this importance is entitled, and that discussion would be carried on under the motion which has been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out that this matter was dealt with within the last few days, in general, in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) as reported at page 2623 of Hansard of April 13, in these words:
"and this house further regrets that the government has failed to present to parliament a

planned financial and economic program designed to develop the economic health of the nation by, among other things-
And these are almost the words spoken by the hon. member for Assiniboia today:
- (a) reversing the trend of rising interest rates
(b) establishing a capital gains tax".
This question of the rising rate of interest has already been dealt with; and in addition it was our intention on Monday next to move to go into supply. We were prepared to move on Monday in that direction. We were prepared to go ahead, and move to go into supply. The suggestion was made by the opposition that in view of the fact that internal arrangements made it necessary for the Leader of the Opposition to be in another part of the country on that date, the opposition would sooner not have the motion made on Monday. However, in view of the argument which has been advanced I suggest that every opportunity will be given on Monday. We will certainly provide a motion to go into supply, so the argument advanced by the hon. member for Laurier is met. We are not going to have to wait until Wednesday or even Thursday of next week; on Monday we can move to go into supply. I suggest first that the motion made is out of order in that it contravenes the rule that discussion on a matter cannot be brought up twice in the same session, particularly when it is embodied in an amendment, and second that we will give all hon. members every opportunity on Monday to do that which they desire to do.

If the motion by the hon. member for Assiniboia is ruled out of order by you, sir, perhaps we could have a supply motion on Monday, because I would not like a request which I made in all good faith and which had nothing to do with the situation which developed yesterday to prevent the house from discussing such an important matter as a tight money policy which has resulted in the high interest rates reached yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Ottawa West asked me a question with regard to an international conference on lead and zinc and I promised to reply, which I am now prepared to do.
A meeting of the United Nations lead and zinc committee will commence on April 28 in New York. It is expected to last three days and to concentrate its attention upon developments since the previous conference, which was held in Geneva last November. In the first days of the following week there will be an inaugural meeting of a continuing lead and zinc study group which it may be decided shall supersede the existing committee.
The first object of these meetings will be to assess the demand and supply situation in these metals, to endeavour to reach a common understanding regarding present trends, to establish what may be the cause of any difficulties confronting the world industry and to discuss various governments' viewpoints on the necessity and possibility of any remedial action. It would also be appropriate for the conference to give its attention to the possibility of improving the extent and currency of statistical information and to the factors which affect levels of consumption.
The existing surplus situation in these metals was complicated by the action of the United States government in October of last year to restrict imports of lead and zinc in metal and concentrate forms to 80 per cent of the average United States imports during the five years ending in 1957. At the Geneva conference last November this action on the part of the United States was the object of 66968-9-192}
Inquiries of the Ministry criticism by many members of the conference. The Canadian government's views regarding the United States import quotas are well known to the house. Canadian objections have been expressed in a formal exchange of notes. Canadian rights to compensation for impairment of important tariff concessions by the United States under GATT have been reserved. This matter was also examined in January in the joint United States-Canada committee on trade and economic problems, as reported in the communique issued at the end of those meetings. Our position is unchanged.
The Canadian delegation will again make it clear that Canada is willing to explore the necessity for and possibility of an international agreement, but that to be acceptable to Canada any such agreement must find wide support with all major importing and exporting countries playing their full part.
I have received a number of representations from Canadian industry and I have noted the position taken by the Canadian metal mining association endorsing the stand taken by the Canadian delegation at the Geneva meetings. A strong delegation will attend from Canada comprised of senior official experts and accompanied by leading businessmen from the Canadian industry as advisers.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Rea in the chair.

Administration branch-
1.	Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $747,531.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, representing as I do a largely rural constituency, I could not let the Department of Agriculture estimates go by without saying a few words on the problems of a very important sector of our national economy.
In my first speech here, last year, I outlined the history of colonization in the Saguenay district and, if I remember well, I mentioned that our economy was based largely on agricultural production. With the industrialization which came later on, the surplus of our population found a ready market and formed the elements of a working class still imbued with rural spirit, and which is therefore different from the ordinary working class found in large cities. Agricultural production in the constituency of Chicoutimi is based on the dairy industry, and that is why farmers in my area are particularly affected by surplus production in that field.
Like the hon. member for Kent (N.B.) (Mr. Michaud), I am very grateful to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for disregarding certain advice that support prices on all dairy products be removed. The considerable surplus of milk powder now glutting the market is precisely a result of a support price fixed at too high a level. That is why I feel that the decision to lower that support price is wise, since it will allow us to dispose of those surpluses, while increasing cheese production for which the market is now excellent.
I am glad to point out here the initiative taken by the Agricultural Co-operative Society of Chicoutimi which, even before being informed of the ministerial decision, had taken steps to cut down its milk powder production and increase its cheese production. Initiatives of that type on the part of private enterprise will no doubt help the government re-establish a fair balance in the production of dairy products.

The Minister of Agriculture must also be congratulated for having granted a subsidy of 25 cents per hundred pounds on all milk delivered to processing plants. To a certain extent, this subsidy will help narrow the gap between the price paid to suppliers for whole milk and the price paid to suppliers at processing plants.
Mr. Chairman, the study of these estimates gives me an opportunity to register a protest, on behalf of Quebec cheese producers who, under the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act, are being paid one half cent less per pound than Ontario producers. I realize that such an injustice is not intentional, but that it is the accidental result of statistics compiled for the last ten years. However, I think the minister should introduce the necessary legislation to rectify this abnormal situation where producers living closer to distribution and export outlets are receiving less than those living farther.
Mr. Chairman, a good many farmers in my constituency have to do some woodcutting to earn enough to meet their family's needs. The main demand is for pulpwood, which is bought by the large paper mills. It is known that there is a certain slowdown in the production and sales of pulpwood, but the fact remains that our larger mills could easily absorb the ten thousand odd cords of pulpwood that are cut by our settlers and farmers. Due to certain misunderstandings, sales have slowed down; moreover, a Department of Justice investigation has revealed the existence of a vast conspiration, among the big corporations, to cheat farmers out of this important part of their income. I therefore hope that the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act will also be made applicable to wood that is cut by settlers and farmers, so that in the future, they will be assured of a minimum return for their efforts.
Before closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I also, on behalf of my constituents, urge that soil classification and analysis be carried out as soon as possible, as this would enable us to draw up an overall plan for maximum land use. At the present time, because no such plan exists, certain settlers are living on marginal lands that should have remained part of the forest industry, and these people merely eke out a living because their income is comparable to the land prevailing in underdeveloped countries, and they are a problem for all the public and private charity groups.
Then, in order to protect our cattle which represent a major part of our rural inheritance, I wish that necessary steps be taken to fight brucellosis, which is responsible for great losses.

Mr. Chairman, having expressed my opinion concerning agriculture a few weeks ago, it was certainly not my intention to take part again in the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness). However, following the statement he made yesterday, I can't help making a few comments.
First of all, I must say to the minister that we sympathize with him because he seems to be going through a critical period. We wish nevertheless to show him our good will and to put the best of our knowledge at his disposal in order to help him settle the problems which face the farm industry and whose consequences have been felt for some time.
Following the minister's statement, I was most surprised by the speeches made by government members from the province of Quebec. They made certain comments on the minister's statement, and their remarks were mostly congratulatory.
The minister was praised for having granted a 25 cent subsidy for every hundredweight of milk intended to be used for the production of cheese or skim-milk. That is all that was said. No comment was made on the price of milk powder and I think I can even state that not a single member on the government side understood the minister's statement, particularly as far as the price of milk powder is concerned.
As a matter of fact, the minister's statement, of which I am giving only a summary and not a literal translation, is to the effect that the price of milk powder has been reduced from 15 cents to 10 cents per pound, no mention whatever being made of the quality of the product. Only skim milk powder is mentioned in the minister's statement.
However, we know there are two types of milk powder: one produced by the spray process and the other by the roller process. We are just being told that milk powder will be reduced from 15 cents to 10 cents per pound, with no mention of what the price will be for roller processed milk powder. However, Conservative members have praised the minister, without making out what his statement meant. What will be the results of such a policy? I think that the lower price for milk powder will immediately result in the loss of hundreds of thousands of dollars for industrialists and manufacturers, since we are told about this lower price for milk powder only six days before the first of May.
Supply-Agriculture
Manufacturers have large stocks in their warehouses and tomorrow, that is on May 1, at what price will milk powder be sold? Maybe 5 cents, maybe 6 cents, maybe 8 cents, I hope. The blunt fact is that manufacturers are going to lose hundreds of thousands of dollars. And what about the losses the farmers will sustain?
The minister says that the price of milk powder will be reduced from 15 cents to 10 cents a pound. That does not seem, to be serious. He made that statement with disconcerting assurance in about the same frame of mind as the Minister of Finance when he announced his tax boosts.
This policy will have the following effect on farmers: a reduction of 15 cents per hundred pounds of milk powder will be tantamount to a reduction of 40 to 50 cents per hundred pounds of milk.
Last night I got in touch with manufacturers so as to find out what they thought of this policy. It is true that there will be a subsidy of 25 cents per hundredweight, so that, officially, the price of milk powder will be 15 cents. But what happens then to the manufacturer? He will have to take whatever price he can get for his milk powder. Then, he will reduce the price he pays per hundredweight to make up for the lower price he gets for his milk powder.
Manufacturers told me last night that they would lower their purchase price by 40 to 50 cents. This is in addition to last year's price reduction.
Everybody wants to rescue the farmers, to save the Quebec dairy industry! Last year, in our area, milk was selling at $2.90 per hundredweight in the summer and $3 in the winter. Officially, the price should come down to $2.90 on May 1 next. We do hope it is not going to fall below that level.
Now if we examine the purport of the minister's statement and if we try to determine the economic impact of that price change, we find that the government will have to spend from $15 million to $17 million to pay that 25 cent premium per hundred pounds of milk. The spending of $15 to $17 million to protect an economic sector such as agriculture is not too important. What is more serious is what the farmers will be losing. The production of milk in Canada for industrial use is estimated at approximately 7 billion pounds, and we will have to pay 25 cents per hundredweight of milk, which means that the government will have to spend from $15 to $17 million.
On the other hand, if manufacturers of milk powder cut the price by 40 cents to 50 cents per hundredweight of milk, what will be the cost to farmers? Let us take the

Supply-Agriculture
same quantity of milk and let us reduce its price to 40 cents per hundredweight, and we arrive at an amount of $30 to $32 million; such is the loss farmers will suffer as a consequence of the announcement just made by the Minister of Agriculture. Farmers will thus lose 30 million while getting 17 million dollars. Then the Conservative members will come and say in the house: "We are saving the dairy industry: we are giving farmers 17 million dollars."
The manufacturer is then asked to report to the Minister of Agriculture on the quantity of milk he receives for the production of milk powder or cheese. This is another inconvenience which the manufacturer does not like too much but he will supply those reports willingly because he is quite as interested as the minister, and even more so, in saving the farming class.
Yet, the Catholic Farmers' Union (Union catholique des cultivateurs) had made some suggestions and I am surprised to find that hon. members from the province of Quebec who rose yesterday did not mention those suggestions of the professional farmers association in the province of Quebec. None of them mentioned the wishes of our farming population. That is why I am pleased to inform the house of proposals made in this respect.
I shall quote an item by Mr. Guy Hamel, published in L'Action Catholique. The author reports the words of Mr. Lemoine during a meeting of the joint committee of the U.C.C. and the federated co-operatives with the Minister of Agriculture here in Ottawa. Mr. Lemoine said:
Is Mr. Lemoine their president?

Mr. Lemoine is the general president of U.C.C. and he said:
Mr. Lemoine has pointed out that prices asked in Quebec are not based on western grain prices or on the inefficiency of some producers, but on the average Quebec farm unit.
"It is not a premium on inefficiency and routine that we want; we merely want the serious farmer to be able to make a living." He added that the dairy producer was the one who, up to now, had cost the least money to the government of Canada and that he should not have to be penalized or forgotten simply because he might have failed to state his case forcibly enough.
The program suggested to the government was something like this. It is outlined in an article by the same writer, published in L'Action Catholique, stating that the con-

tract which the government should sign was a contract with milk powder producers, whereby the government would agree-
... to buy unsold production at a floor price if, at the end of each month, the producer can show that he has produced 10 per cent less than the corresponding month of the previous year. Thus the surplus production of milk powder would decrease by 10 per cent and the industry would be forced to diversify its production.
2.	The government would pay a subsidy to the producers to make up for any loss on the floor price.
Earlier there had been a reference to a subsidy of 40 cents a hundred pounds instead of 25 cents.
3.	The government would get the industry to sign an agreement to decrease their production of milk powder by 10 per cent a year.
Thus, the industry would be assured of a reasonable profit margin, and production would be directed towards other sectors at the rate of 10 per cent a year.
That was a wise suggestion, and it would not have complicated the useful production control procedures which are being planned, according to minister's statement of yesterday.
Mr. Chairman, I could comment on many other subjects, but I will only deal with the price support policy in regard to hogs and poultry.
The suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture to change the support price for hogs shows that the price support policy has not achieved the purpose for which that act was passed. After being in effect for two years, that law is already obsolete, and yesterday, the minister broke the very law he proposed himself barely two years ago.
A few months from now, he will be amending the price support legislation on pork so as to lower the price from $25 to $23.65. What, again, will be the result of such a policy? First, the price of pork will drop below the present level, because the government intends to stop buying and storing pork; instead, it will pay compensation to restore the difference between the free market price and the price that will be in force next October, that is $23.65.
The other result will be to destroy the balance between the price of fowl and beef in relation to pork. This will cause a general drop in the price of other products.
However, there is one advantage to this plan: it will protect the professional farmer. The present government's price support policy

has caused great harm to the farmers while helping the integrators. And the Minister of Agriculture has shown a serious lack of foresight in enacting this legislation without providing a means of preventing integrators from sharing in the support price policy. I therefore urge him to consider the matter further, with a view to protecting farmers and family farms by ensuring that price supports work not against them, but to their advantage.
We can see what is happening in the agricultural industry. Between 90 and 95 per cent of the production of broilers is dependent on feed manufacturers and operators of meat packing plants. Today, a farmer cannot produce on his own, because production is controlled. I ask the minister to consider the act and to put forth an amendment to give better protection to professional farmers. Last year, the price of broilers was from 16 to 17 cents a pound and in January of this year, from 14 to 16 cents a pound, while the price of turkey varied from 22 to 28 cents a pound, according to grade and weight.
Why should the government not make compensation payments for poultry products like broilers, chickens and turkey? Why does it not prohibit poultry meat imports from the United States?
Last year, we imported $5,408,000 worth of turkey meat or poultry parts; in fact, since 1957, the government has issued 89 import permits for various poultry meats.
I do not know the total quantity of poultry meat that was imported last year, but I have here that of various poultry meats imported under the 89 permits issued between July 1957 to May 30, 1958; we then imported
1,576,000	pounds of poultry meat, apart from the poultry imported since May 1958, when import permits were revoked.
The same goes for broiler chickens. I do not know the quantities of broilers that have been imported, because this kind of imports does not require any permit.
As far as the prospects of the poultry industry are concerned, I must say they are not very promising, since, according to the March edition of L'Actualite economique, the production of broilers would increase by 62 per cent over the same period last year. As far as the production of heavy turkeys is concerned, it will increase by 100 per cent, while that of light turkeys will increase by 4 per cent; it means that during the coming year, the price of poultry will be lower than last year. Besides the price of milk is being reduced as well as the price of pork, etc.
Supply-Agriculture
In the last few months the Minister of Agriculture also made statements to the effect that unless farmers curtailed their production, this government would have to take severe steps either by lowering support prices or, if necessary, by controlling production. How could he induce farmers to reduce production at a time when they are forced to increase it in order to lessen production costs which are already too high? When the government asks farmers to reduce their production, does it mean the big farmer or the small farmer, or does it mean the contract farmer?
Has anything been done to dispose of dairy products surpluses, or hog surpluses and especially of milk powder surpluses? Nothing is left undone to solve the problems of western farmers, who are granted subsidies for their wheat production. Recently they received a $40 million grant from the government, to make up for the low prices they get for their grain, and we congratulate the government for doing so.
And yet western farmers are not satisfied, because a number of them will have to quit the farm, as will one third of Quebec farmers a year or two hence, unless farming conditions are improved in this country.
This year, the intention seems to be to have eastern farmers pay certain premiums or grants which we will be required to pay to some industries, coal or gold mining, in particular.
According to Mr. Mel Andal, who appeared before the Senate committee on soil utilization, one third of the 575,000 Canadian farms are uneconomic units, inhabited by 2,746,000 persons. Of that total number, 55,000 farms located in the prairies are made up of less than 130 acres, and their operation cannot provide a decent standard of living for their owners. In addition, there are in the eastern part of this country 187,000 farms comprising less than 70 acres of improved land. The farmers who operate those farms cannot get a return which would enable them to meet the needs of their families.
The best proof of that statement was given the other day at a sitting of the committee on agriculture where the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) asked for detailed information concerning the percentage of western farmers and eastern farmers who pay income tax.

Supply-Agriculture
At this stage, I should like to read an article published in La Presse, on April 8, 1959, and I quote:
Statistics show that more than 60 per cent of farmers who pay income tax live in Alberta and Saskatchewan, he said.
Of course, the reference here was to the hon. member for Port Arthur.
Western farmers are rather resentful about it. They can hardly account for the fact that only recently 20,000 Saskatchewan farmers paid this tax while only 780 in Quebec did so.
Mr. J. Gear McEntyre, deputy minister of the Taxation Division in the Department of National Revenue, replied that agriculture in the province of Quebec is just sufficient to provide a livelihood for those engaged in it. Returns were checked, but investigations have borne out that most of the incomes in question were not taxable. According to a survey conducted ten years ago, the average farmer's income in eastern Canada is well below the level of taxable income.
That did not prevent Mr. Fisher from saying that Quebec farmers were making good money cutting pulpwood.
Mr. Chairman, if Quebec farmers do not pay any income tax it is simply because they do not earn enough.
On the other hand, if the hon. member for Port Arthur thinks that our farmers are getting rich cutting wood in the forest in the winter months, I would suggest that he go out to the Abitibi area in Quebec, as well as the maritimes, and see how much those people are getting for their pulpwood.
Mr. Chairman, it will be remembered that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated in Rimouski that a support price would be placed under pulpwood. However, we never hear anything about it any more, and members on the government side who consider themselves economists never say a word about it either.
The farm policy of the Conservative government is a complete wash-out that will lead thousands of farmers into bankruptcy, because of the price reduction affecting all farm products, especially in eastern Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I agree that the present surplus is embarrassing to the Minister of Agriculture. However, that situation is the result of the fine promises made by Conservative candidates during last elections. Farmers had then been promised their share of the national income, and a refund to each family of the excess $120 that the Liberal government was taking out of their pockets each year.
While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) forecasts a general recovery in

every economic and industrial sector, the Conservative government, through its farm policy, is taking the bread out of the mouth of farmers and their families.
On April 14 last, L'Action Catholique published an editorial which sums up my position perfectly, and which says:
The problem of the dairy industry cannot be considered by itself, outside the economic and social context of which it is the key. If there is a depression in that sector, the whole of Quebec's agriculture will be hit by that depression at a time when, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), a general recovery is starting in other sectors of our economy.
Mr. Chairman, I ask all hon. members from the province of Quebec, and others from eastern Canada, to mark the following paragraph:
That present surpluses are a matter of embarrassment for the government is easy to understand. But has any effort been made to dispose of them, that is an effort even remotely comparable to those made on behalf of wheat producers?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to inform the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.

I think I should say something now to dispel the complete misconception which the hon. member who has just spoken evidently has with regard to the new stabilization program for dairy products and with regard to the stabilization program generally.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska indicated clearly that he has not understood the import of the announcement I made yesterday; and in addition, of course, the figures he produced are complete nonsense. They are worse than those produced by the Martin bureau of statistics. They are complete nonsense and bear no relationship to the facts, and for that reason I think I should set the record straight.
The 25 cents per hundred pounds mentioned in the statement yesterday is not being paid to the manufacturers, as the hon. member seems to think. It is being paid to the producers. It will be paid directly to the farmers; therefore as far as people sending milk to the cheese factories are concerned, they will get more money for their milk than they were receiving formerly, instead of taking a loss on it. As far as people delivering milk for general manufacture are concerned, rather than a loss of 40 or 50 cents a hundred pounds the biggest reduction they

should get in any circumstances should he 15 cents per hundred pounds, and in many cases there should be no reduction at all. The hon. member evidently does not understand the complexities of the milk business, in addition to failing to understand, perhaps deliberately, the statement I made yesterday.
The hon. member also said that the prices of all agricultural products in Quebec had gone down, apparently in an effort to convey the impression that they had gone down since this government took office. Actually the price of nearly every agricultural product has gone up since this government came to power. If the hon. member will look at the statistics with regard to the prices of agricultural products during the past year as compared to those received when the Liberal government was in power he will find that there has been a very material improvement. He will also find that last year the farmers of Quebec received a larger cash income than they had ever received in any previous year in history. In addition, as I said, the prices they received for most of their products were considerably better than they had been when the Liberals were in power.

Mr. Chairman, may I direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture?
I fully understand the statement he made yesterday and I know full well that 25 cents per hundred pounds of milk will be paid to the farmers. I would like to know whether the manufacturer will have to pay the minimum price for milk or if he will be free to set his own price. I know very well that the farmer will get 25 cents and that the price is not supposed to go down by more than 5 cents a hundred pounds for the manufacture of milk powder. But the manufacturer will not be in a position to sell milk powder at a lower price; consequently he will set the price of milk according to the price of milk powder. That is the way I understand the situation.
Now, the Minister of Agriculture says that the farmer got more cash in 1958 than he ever did in previous years. I admit that the income from the sale of agricultural products has increased in 1958.
Hear, hear.

Very well, I accept the
cheers of the hon. members on the government side. However, I must add that it is not the farmers, but the integrators who got the most money, both in Quebec province and in Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed the pleasure of asking a question of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger)?

Please do.

What action does he suggest to dispose of the overproduction of milk powder that now exists in Canada, and what does he think of milk powder companies who were aware of the present overproduction situation? Were such companies helping the farmers, or were they considering their own interests. I should very much appreciate an answer to that.

If there had been time, I would have answered the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Mr. Chairman, as the representative of a mostly rural constituency, may I take a few minutes of the time of this committee at this point in the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to submit a few requests that have been made by farm organizations of my constituency, and, at the same time, to express to the minister my satisfaction for the statements he made yesterday about the support price for the products of the dairy industry.
I believe I am right, Mr. Chairman, in saying this, because the price that will be guaranteed for the next twelve months in this regard meets the wish expressed by the heads of the province of Quebec farm association, and the U.C.C. who recently came to the committee on agriculture to submit their brief, and acknowledged that the government should check the powdered milk production because of the rather heavy stocks of that product.

Supp ly-A griculture
I also want to express, on behalf of those people in my riding who follow that profession, all my appreciation to the hon. Minister of Agriculture for the generous manner in which he, as well as hon. members of this house and the farmers' unions concerned, co-operated in the study of the suggestions submitted and the brief presented to him, in view of obtaining a stable and proper price level.
I sometimes wonder, Mr. Chairman, if other classes in society realize the considerable work which must be done on a farm in order to make it yield enough to allow a family to live in reasonable comfort.
I am myself a farmer's son, living in a parish which is essentially a farming district. I know that, unlike a good many city people who work only five days a week, these people have to toil seven days a week and, in many cases, require the help of other members of the family, even school children, in order to get things done.
For a good many farmers the revenue obtained from the sale of dairy products is not enough; they have to make up for it by seeking work outside the additional revenue they need to survive. Some of them take jobs in logging camps, others earn extra money by raising hogs, poultry or from a maple bush, sometimes also by very carefully making use of their wood lots. Let us stop and consider for a moment the degree of insecurity the farmer has to face, because of possible losses, which quite frequently occur.
Many farmers in my riding were affected this year by the loss of some of their cattle in the outbreak of rabies. I wish to express my appreciation to the minister for the work done to check this disease by having dogs vaccinated. But there is still an enemy that causes great concern: the fox. A great many of my constituents have told me about that animal which remains in the vicinity of farm buildings, even refusing to run away from man, a behaviour which is certainly contrary to its normal wild instincts and denotes symptoms of the disease in its latent form.
While I was in my riding last week-end,
I got a phone call from the mayor of St. Gilbert who told me that a farmer had lost an animal which, according to the veterinary, had probably been bitten by a fox that had caused great damage a few days before in the hen-house of that farmer.

I received another letter this week from a St. Augustin farmer who according to the veterinary's report, suffered a similar loss.
I mention those cases, Mr. Chairman, to acquaint the government with this situation and enable it to study the problem which could be solved perhaps by providing a bounty to promote fox hunting.
I made those few remarks so that everyone may realize the plight of this class of workers referred to yesterday by my deskmate in this house, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Rogers) when he said:
(Text):
As a matter of fact, it seems to be an established fact that farm prices are the first to go down and the last to go up.
(Translation):
Well, it really makes you think.
Recently, I received from the secretary of the Quebec district association of Ayrshire cattle breeders, a resolution passed at a general meeting asking the government to give effect to the latest requests for herd "control". According to information given to this house by the minister, this temporary delay has been caused by a shortage of staff. I have no doubt that even if this means increasing the staff, there will be no difficulty involved in giving effect to these requests from the farmers, who are anxious to follow the instructions given by their technical advisors, namely the agronomists, so as to improve their herds. In closing, I wish to express my great appreciation to the government for the attention it has been giving to the farmers, so as to enable them to take their rightful place in Canada's economy.

Mr. Chairman, I hope you will allow me to take up a few minutes of the committee's time to make my humble contribution to this discussion. I should like to make it known to the committee at the outset that I have no intention, in my brief remarks, to indulge in what is commonly known as petty politics.
It is my aim to be as realistic as possible and to examine briefly the various aspects of the difficult problems facing the Minister of Agriculture and the government in the management of the country.
Since my election to this house last May, I have been listening closely to most of the speeches made by hon. members. As far as I am concerned, this is the third time I have had the opportunity to speak.

I listened to the criticism of the opposition; I listened to members from all the provinces of our country who did their utmost to draw attention to their respective problems and those that are common to the whole nation.
Mr. Chairman, a few weeks ago, I listened to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) who tried to draw a gloomy picture of agriculture under the Conservative government. And I wish to repeat once more-and I do not want to indulge in politics but only make sure that the fact is recorded that economic crises have not always been the outcome of Conservative governments-that, if at the present time, we have an economic recession which, fortunately, is about to disappear, the Conservatives are not responsible.
Mr. Chairman, a few days before the 1930 election, perhaps some members now sitting in this house were not old enough to realize the economic situation of the time, but the one who is talking to you was then head of a family and was operating a farm.
Prior to the 1930 election-and the Conservatives were not in power at the time, it was the Liberal party, and it had been in power, I believe, since 1921-butter was selling for 18 to 20 cents a pound; eggs, 12 to 15 cents a dozen; pork, 10 to 12 cents a pound; beef, 8 to 10 cents a pound. The worker earned an average salary of $1.50 to $2 a day to provide for the needs of his family.
I do not think the figures I have just quoted are indicative of a fruitful administration, and the legacy it left, after the 1930 election, was not a very enviable economic situation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not like to hand out compliments indiscriminately, but I believe it is worth noting, even briefly, that the hon. Minister of Agriculture deserves congratulations for the ability, the tact and the practical leadership he has shown a few days ago, when he decided to lower the support prices for certain agricultural products, a decision he announced to the house yesterday.
Starting October 1 the price of hogs will be reduced by one dollar and some cents a hundredweight; however, a subsidy equal to the former price will be paid to the average farmer. That is where, Mr. Chairman, we see the value of the system that the Minister of Agriculture is using to discourage
Supply-A griculture
and destroy vertical integration, i.e. by discouraging those who make a large business of hog raising and production. Of course, these are private undertakings on which the government has no direct control, because the government cannot stop a large feed manufacturer from setting up hog raising farms able to market an unusual number of pigs each year. But, in a general way, the former system, with fixed support prices far from discouraging integration, favoured it because, no matter how many hogs each producer put on the market, he received a uniform price on the whole, for his product; he received the same support price as the smaller producer.
Not very long ago, Mr. Chairman, I received a letter from a farmer in my riding who hinted in rather broad and uncertain terms, that the farm group, the average producer, who has a family living and makes a living out of farming, that the Minister of Agriculture should adopt a policy that would establish a distinction between the professional producer and the man who takes to hog raising on an integrated basis.
In La Terre de chez nous, on April 8, 1959, there was an editorial by Mr. Louis-Philippe Poulin, entitled "Hog prices policy". Mr. Poulin said in this editorial among other things:
The application of deficiency payments to a specific number of hogs per farm seems to us to be much more effective, even though such a system gives rise to some problems.
At the outset of his article, the author says:
The average farmer must derive advantages from it.
In brief, the article of Mr. Poulin is in favour of the policy and of the prices which were announced to us yesterday by the hon. Minister of Agriculture.
With regard to the support price of butter, we all know that this price is maintained at 64 cents a pound. It is my conviction that on account of his wisdom and competence the hon. Minister of Agriculture has not been maintaining the support price of butter at such a level to please those who produce this product. Indeed, he has shown realism, since statistics show that, as of January 1, 1955, we had in stock 91,151,000 pounds of butter, compared with 69,899,000 pounds as of January 1, 1958. If you take into account the fact that our population was
15,803,000	inhabitants in 1955, when our stocks of butter reached 91,151,000 pounds and the fact that our population has now increased to 17,000,000, we can reach the conclusion that present stocks of butter, proportionately and on the basis of the individual

Supply-Agriculture
average, are much less substantial than they were in 1954 and 1955. In my opinion, the Minister of Agriculture has shown wisdom in continuing to encourage the manufacturers of butter to continue their production. Undoubtedly, neither the farmers nor the producers of butter will get rich on 64 cents a pound. Nevertheless, this price will enable the average farmer to have from his dairy herd, a reasonable if not a big return.
Mr. Chairman, I suppose my hon. friend, the member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) expects me to talk about milk powder. The hon. member's wish will be fulfilled, as I intend to speak on this matter. However, before I undertake a detailed analysis of the matter, I would like to stress the fact that I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say that the policy of the hon. Minister of Agriculture as far as powdered milk is concerned, answered a need and showed that he has a good deal of practical common sense when it comes to implementing his price support policy.
Powdered milk is not used very much in Canada. It is also a product for which there is little demand on the export markets and which is perishable. After a few months, it loses much of its value and taste and it would certainly not be wise to maintain its present level of production in Quebec and Ontario.
Mr. Chairman, it is a known fact that in everything we reap as we sow, and the complication now arising in relation to the price of milk powder is the result of the fact that in 1957, the government then in power, without being even requested to set a minimum price for milk powder, introduced a 17 cent a pound support price. What happened then? In the province of Quebec alone, we saw a score of new industries develop and we saw the work of many cooperative members being sabotaged by people who had set their minds to make money through the processing of milk into powder. We have also farm organizations, butter and cheese co-operatives, being crushed or blotted out. We have seen them disappear and replaced by milk powder producers who had one purpose, that of making money with their plants. That brings me, Mr. Chairman, to what I said a moment ago. We are reaping what we have sown. In 1957, we adopted a policy which did not correspond to a need and, unfortunately, we are reaping today the nefarious effects of

that policy which was devoid of practical common sense.
That reminds me, Mr. Chairman, of the story of a fellow going out for a walk on a fine day; caught in a storm and having no umbrella, be must at least partially suffer the nefarious effects of the weather.
Mr. Chairman, there was fair sailing when the Canadian government established a support price for milk powder at 17 cents a pound. Our farmers went ahead producing milk powder at that time, but today, the storm had to come down, because no government with any sense of responsibility can continue to favour production of a commodity which being perishable, is hardly fit for export, and whose output is far in excess of domestic consumption.
That does not justify the government giving away milk powder.

Mr. Chairman, I must commend the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud) for the speech he made yesterday in this house. The hon. gentleman showed a lot of common sense; he is a professional farmer like myself, and a credit to his calling. The hon. member was frank enough not to commend the Minister of Agriculture, but to formally state his approval of the healthy policy of the Minister of Agriculture. As recorded on page 2 of the English appendix to Hansard of April 23, 1959, the hon. member said:
And I am sure that dairy farmers will be pleased to hear that the government intends to maintain at 64 cents a pound the support price on butter production.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, probably in good faith, claims that Conservative members do not understand a thing about agriculture nor about the acute problems which now face the farming industry.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I did not say that government members do not understand the problems of the agricultural industry. I said Conservative members had not understood the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture about milk powder.

Mr. Chairman, until I have proof of the contrary, and until I have read in Hansard the speech of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, I accept his correction.

Mr. Chairman ...

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, before recess, I dealt only with the latest statement of the Minister of Agriculture on support prices for agricultural products. I now wish to discuss, as briefly as possible, some problems relating to agriculture in Canada. Before doing so, however, may I once again urge the Minister of Agriculture to maintain his price support policy, which gives encouragement to the agricultural class, to average producers and to heads of families. I also ask the minister to use the strictest methods to curb those who have been practising integration, whether in hog raising, poultry raising or milk powder production. May the minister's policy be such as to deter people who, in the past, have pushed integration too far and have caused untold harm to farmers across Canada.
I think I mentioned, at the beginning of my remarks, that I listened closely to most speeches made in this house since my election to parliament in Ottawa, in May 1958. This has made me realize that the agricultural problem is not the least problem facing the federal government; indeed, it is the government's responsibility to give special consideration to a great many problems.
I have been hearing hon. members from other provinces in western Canada setting forth the demands of their constituents, and I realize, Mr. Chairman, that there are very great problems to be solved in that section of the country. I have also been aware for many years that eastern Canada faces serious problems. When speaking of the west, I presume this should include Manitoba and the other provinces up to the Pacific, including British Columbia; and when speaking of the east we mean Ontario and Quebec right down to the Atlantic.
Supp ly-A griculture
However, Mr. Chairman, my purpose this afternoon is to discuss the acute problems affecting Canada's far eastern section. By that I mean the area from Quebec city eastward. It may be that many hon. members from western Canada know absolutely nothing about the great natural difficulties which confront the farmers of that area, the far eastern part of Canada, in the discharge of their occupation.
The land of my constituency is not naturally fertile and is often rocky in many areas. The climate is severe; our winters are very cold and very hard. Hon. members might be surprised to know that in my parish, no later than last Monday, I saw snow banks 5 to 7 feet deep along the roads. In fact, at this time of the year, owners of dairy herds still have to keep the herds in the stable and feed them. Summer is very short for the growing season and the grazing season is limited to two months, that is from June 15 to August 15. Thus, Mr. Chairman, it is impossible to imagine all the sacrifices and the hard work, the problems of all kinds to which the pioneers in our region were subjected when they had to clear the land to get tillable soil fertile enough to provide a living for the families of eastern Canada.
Those are problems that the federal government must not ignore. Farmers of eastern Canada, farmers in the area east of Quebec city must receive at all times and continue to receive from this government the necessary encouragement to maintain family farming. We do not have many industries and being located as far as we are from large centres, we find transportation a problem. However, it is important that the authorities be made aware of their responsibilities. We must not forsake this region which was conquered with sweat and sacrifice just because it is far from large centres or because the climate is not favourable to agriculture. It is essential that the average farmer, the producer, the head of the family, be in a position to increase his production and receive fair prices for his products.
Our farmers should be made to feel that they can keep their trust in established authority; they must continue giving their children some education; they must continue impressing upon the masses, and upon their daughters and their sons, the patriotic spirit which should be nurtured by every good citizen in this country. The sons of farmers

Supply-Agriculture
should remain on the land; and that area which, perhaps, has not been conquered as easily as others should again receive encouragement from the federal government and all right-thinking people who want our great country to be prosperous, progressive and happy.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to mention some needs of the farming people in the area I just mentioned. Our soil does not favour seed grain production, and farmers in the eastern part of the province must buy those seeds from producers either in the other eastern parts of this country or in the west. Since, as I said a moment ago, distances are long and freight rates are very high, the Department of Agriculture should consider the possibility of granting subsidies in such a way as to relieve the cost of freight rates for seed grain.
Second, as the soil is not naturally fertile, we must-and I repeat Mr. Chairman, we must-as I am one of those who sire concerned with small farming, one of those who buy seed grain and who buy fertilizers-buy fertilizers; but, at the present time, because of freight rates, the cost of those products is very high indeed.
The government could also grant a fairly substantial subsidy for the transportation of calcereous ameliorators. This is the name given to ground limestone, commonly known as "calco". Added to our soil, that product has given excellent results in the past. But, unfortunately, there again, its cost price, once it gets to our farms, is still too high for many of our farmers. I believe, if I am not carrying my argument too far, that the federal government could perhaps, authorize an investigation of the fertilizer industry-
