Mr. Chairman, as this session progresses and as the minister makes one announcement after another, it becomes more and more clear that the government has abandoned its agricultural policy as set forth in the recent election campaigns. When the Prime Minister was in the opposition for many years he spoke, as did many of the rest of us, in favour of parity prices. It was the policy of the Conservative party before the election in 1957 to establish a system of support prices in this country based on a parity relationship. In the Conservative handbook for the 1957 election it

is reported that regular motions have been introduced into the house by Mr. Diefen-baker in order to secure for the farmer a more satisfactory share of the national income.
That is one quotation and I have many others here. I will put a few of them on the record but they are all along the same line. When the Prime Minister spoke on June 8, 1957, he is reported by the Canadian Press as promising that if a Conservative government were elected he would call a September session of parliament to set up a system of floor prices for agricultural products based on parity. Well, we have had some indications this session that the present Minister of Agriculture is basically carrying out the same kind of program that we have had with previous ministers of agriculture. We have had certain support prices for agricultural products; the government has failed to obtain markets for products at the support prices and immediately the support price has been cut. This announcement was made as far as hog support prices are concerned, that there will be a reduction in the floor price October 1 from $25 a hundredweight to $23.65, basis Toronto.
Then there was the announcement yesterday that the government is reducing the floor price of powdered milk from 15 cents to 10 cents a pound, and that a few months from now the support price will be removed altogether. In its place will be paid a 25 cent per hundred pounds of milk deficiency payment under certain conditions. The total of the government's announcements adds up to lower prices for agricultural commodities.
These announcements have not been supported by the farm organizations. This government is not carrying out the recommendations which have been brought to it by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture or the Ontario milk producers and other farm organizations. Soon after the minister's announcement was made yesterday the following press release was made by the Ontario farmers' union.
Dairy price support levels announced in the House of Commons by agriculture minister Harkness indicate flagrant disregard for the high ideals expressed by the Conservative government in the agricultural prices support legislation enacted in January 1958, said Gordon L. Hill, president of the Ontario farmers' union.
There is Mr. Hill's statement as to what this announcement on dairy support prices means-a flagrant disregard for the high ideals expressed by the Conservative party

in the agricultural prices support legislation enacted in January, 1958. The statement goes on:
"While Mr. Harkness is to be commended for changing the system from market price support to the deficiency payment system in the case of skim milk powder, the amount of deficiency payment is negative and completely ignores increasing farm costs", Mr. Hill said. "In the face of rising operating costs Canadian farmers are expected to hold the line on prices for some commodities and to absorb price cuts on others such as milk powder, and a reduction in the price of milk powder is not in line with the objectives of the act. Rising costs for fertilizer, farm implements, mill feeds, freight rates and other goods and services which farmers must buy have created an impossible situation for the dairyman", said Mr. Hill. He stated that concentrating milk producers, who are already living on the depreciation of their assets, will be forced to seek an additional source of income. This will increase the trend to contract farming and vertical integration wihch is already sounding the death knell of the family type farm.
This is the answer to statements of hon. members opposite that their program has been one to assist and promote the small farmer. Mr. Hill says that this policy of the government will increase the trend to contract farming and vertical integration. The statement concludes with the following:
"A disturbing aspect of the whole situation." Mr. Hill continued, "is that the advisory committee to the stabilization board has been completely ignored. What use is an advisory committee that is not consulted?" Mr. Hill asked.
I think this last statement is a very grave reflection on the attitude of the government. I think it is a rather serious indictment of the way the minister considers this legislation in advance when he has, according to Mr. Hill, failed to have the advisory committee consider this question.

I did not hear all the hon. member has said, but if I may comment on what I understand him as saying now I think that Mr. Hill and every member of the advisory committee will bear me out when I tell him that the committee spent three days discussing this matter of price support for dairy products at its last meeting. They have in fact considered this matter and have been considering it throughout the past year. Then, as I say, they spent three days of their last meeting doing so.
Could the minister say when the last meeting was held?
I think it was about six weeks or two months ago. I cannot be certain how long ago it was.

I appreciate the comment made by the minister. I am not going to dispute it. All I have done is to place in the record the last paragraph of the statement that was
Supply-Agriculture
issued as a result of the announcement yesterday. Perhaps the wording of the announcement might be considered to mean that the recommendations of the advisory board have not been carried out. That may be what it means, although I do not, myself, think so. I took it as meaning that they were not consulted. The minister shakes his head, and I take it, now, that they held a three-day meeting and put forward certain recommendations with regard to which the minister has not taken action.
I note that the minister has not made any comment on that part of the statement issued by Mr. Hill in which he says that the government's policy has shown flagrant disregard of the high ideals expressed in its agricultural prices support legislation, nor on Mr. Hill's statement that the policy ignores increases in farming costs.
There will have to be a good deal of new thought and new ideas placed in the government's agricultural policy if the small farm is to survive in this country. Under the policy announced by the government-a program of lower and lower price supports for agricultural products-the ordinary family farm in this country is facing increasingly great difficulties. We had hoped that the government would take action in other fields. We had hoped that the government would move in the direction set forth in the brief presented by the farm delegation. We still await an announcement by the government, and as the days go on, and as one member of parliament from the prairie provinces after another goes on the record, it is becoming more and more clear to me that a unanimous decision has been taken by the Conservative members from the three prairie provinces that deficiency payments as outlined in the submission of the farm delegation should be opposed and are not in the interest of western agriculture.
We have the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Wheat, oats and barley are not included under its provisions. The government has purchased a number of commodities under the terms of this act, and I submitted a series of questions, to which the minister has provided answers, as to the quantities of the various commodities which have been supported. I think there is a feeling abroad in this country that supports for agricultural products benefit western Canada almost exclusively. There seems to be a feeling that when a farmer gets something it is always the prairie farmer who is on the receiving end. I think the statistics which the Department of Agriculture has produced in this regard are most revealing, because they show that out of a total of $69,814,000 worth of agricultural products purchased by the board

Supp ly-A griculture from April 31, 1958 to December 31, 1958, only some $5,862,000 worth were purchased in the three prairie provinces. Thus, whatever the value the act has been so far, and to whatever extent it provides for some support for agricultural producers from the national treasury, it has in the main benefited farmers outside the prairie provinces. I think that is an additional argument in favour of government action at this time to support, by way of deficiency payment, the prices of western grain.
The government has stated that it has an agricultural policy. Members of the government say that there is an agricultural policy designed to help the small farmer, to give the farmer a greater share of the national income, and to provide prices for agricultural producers which are fair and which bear a fair relationship to cost of production. In fact, I think the program is almost the exact opposite. It is a program which has failed to deal with agricultural surpluses; it is a program which merely mimics the program of the previous administration; it is a program without vision; it is a program which means that in the face of agricultural surpluses the government acts to reduce support prices.
When the Prime Minister met the delegates, and when he spoke in this house a year ago on the dollar an acre program, he said the government had a long term policy, and in that long term program he included just about everything but the kitchen sink. Among the matters he included-and upon which we are now awaiting action-were long term farm credit, crop insurance and some other matters. We await legislation on these subjects with interest. We shall study it very carefully when it is brought before this house, and we shall support it on second reading if we think it is in the best interests of the agricultural community.
But while we are waiting for the government to move in the direction of easing farm credit and bringing in an improved farm credit program, may I point out that the government is allowing interest rates in this country to increase? The government is saying: we intend to provide long term farm credit; but on the other hand it says: let the Bank of Canada discount rate go up to 4.97 per cent; let this result in an increase in the prime interest rate for the banks; let this result in the insurance companies and finance companies across this country being able to increase their charges. Is this tight money policy of the present government-the policy which is now in effect-not increasing charges to the agricultural community of this country? Of course it is. The government talks in one way, and acts in another. It has talked in
IMr. Argue.]

favour of fair prices; it has talked in favour of prices bearing a fair cost relationship, but only yesterday we heard the announcement that the floor price on skinmed milk powder is being reduced.
I think the case which the western producers put before the government was a sound one. I think it was a modest one. It was one which asked for a fair parity price, as the government has promised. It did not ask that all the increases in cost of production should be taken into account, but it said to the government: we want you to take action to maintain the price of wheat, in recent years and today, such as we have enjoyed over an eight-year period from 1947 onwards, and although we shall find it most difficult we are prepared to absorb the increase in the cost ourselves.
In this fair and moderate position which the agricultural producers have taken, when they have looked to this house for members to support them, they have found that the people who have opposed them the most, and consistently opposed them, are the members of parliament from the prairie provinces. They have opposed the case that was put forward by the farm delegation. I do not think I have to quote statements to prove that; Hansard is full of them. The statements are being repeated day after day. Yesterday the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose had this to say, as reported at page 2983 of Hansard:
We are supposed to believe that every member of that delegation was in agreement with deficiency payments. They were not.
Here is another slur on the farm delegation. This is a slur on the farm delegation that came down here-
No, it is not.

-and met in the Chateau Laurier in conference before they prepared their brief, unanimously supported the brief and presented it to the government. And yet a member from the prairie provinces said that a good 50 per cent of them were satisfied with the acreage payments if only we would pay just a little more. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that that statement is just as far wrong and just as misleading as the statement made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson that if you did what the delegation requested all you would do would be to give the farmer with a Cadillac, a Buick. That is a slur, Mr. Chairman, on the agricultural producers of western Canada who are not driving Cadillacs, and the hon. member knows it and, generally speaking, they are not driving Buicks. These people have had an average income in recent years less than the average national income. These extravagant statements are more grist

for the mill; this makes good press copy in eastern Canada but it is a false position for the hon. member to put forward and it is completely inaccurate.
In the years when the hon. member for Essex East sat on the other side of the house with his colleagues the members from the prairie provinces had a different line. They would get up in the house and they would get up back home and they would say, "We are really working for the people we represent; we are trying to do the best we can. But, you know, it is the eastern members we cannot convince. If you would come down and help us convince", as the member for Swift Current-Maple Creek used to say, "the eastern members, we would get somewhere". We not only have a new government in office, we have a complete change in the line; we have a complete change in the attitude. According to the prairie farm delegation, the attitude now is that they received a more sympathetic hearing from eastern members than they received from the prairie members.
Nonsense.
I think it is true. You find that in one report after another. Here is a report by Robert Moon and Ron. Brown.
Oh, oh.

They snicker. I have not the faintest notion what they are laughing about:
Prairie farm delegates Wednesday were becoming openly hostile to the nature of grain deficiency payment replies given them by their western Conservative M.P.'s.
Coming on the heels of Prime Minister Diefenbaker's rejection of immediate payments on Tuesday morning, the rebuffs they were meeting from their own western members came as a shocking aftermath.
I scarcely need to quote from this report. Hansard is full of statements of one member in this house from the prairie provinces that deficiency payments are not the answer; that an acreage payment is the best. Therefore, whether they are hostile or whether it is just strong opposition or whether 50 per cent are in favour of what they are supporting, I will leave it to the people who are affected to decide.
I think there would be a chance for deficiency payments if the members from the prairies in this house were anywhere as nearly ranged in favour of the position taken by the farm delegation as the people on the prairies are at this time. I am certain that if the members of parliament from western Canada would say to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Agriculture, "We want action; we think the farmers have a case for deficiency payments", something would be done; but as long as the members who
Supply-Agriculture
represent the farmers who are directly affected stand up in the house and say their case is not a good one, that half of them do not believe in it and it is not something that is advantageous to the average farmer, then, of course, there is little or no hope that this will be done. What is the excuse?
Will the hon. member permit a question?

I will be very pleased to answer if the hon. member would wait until after the timekeeper over here calls the time. The last time I spoke half of my speech was made up of questions.
These gentlemen say that deficiency payments are not the answer; that if you have a deficiency payment which is paid on the unit of wheat at a certain ceiling, as stated by the brief, you help the big farmers. Oh, how these people want to help the little farmers. Their hearts bleed for the little farmers.
Does yours?

What did they say in the house yesterday? They said, "We want a two-price system; we do not want to get the deficiency payment that is asked for by the western delegates, but we will take a piece of it. We will not take it out of the national treasury but will add it to the price of bread". But when we get the two-price system, if we get it, I ask them if they are going to put a ceiling on the amount that is paid to any farmer who sells wheat, or are they going to do as the Prime Minister said a year ago, that if you increase the price by 50 cents a bushel to provide a two-price system it would add 6J cents to the price of bread.
If we get a two-price system-and I am in favour of it and have been in favour of it for years-do the hon. members say that they will not use it and pay it out on an acreage basis up to 200 acres? No, I am certain they will pay it on the price of a bushel of wheat, where it should be paid, and that is the whole case that is being put forward by the farm delegation.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the agricultural problems facing this country can be solved. The surplus can be disposed of and I would suggest that a food surplus disposal corporation should be established at this time and properly constituted, with a board that would have the power to undertake to sell all of these products and to dispose of these products by contact; that would have the power to obtain other goods in exchange. Call it a barter system, if you like, which is one of the things that has worked in the United States. This disposal corporation

Supp ly-A griculture
should dispose of some of these products byproviding that they be used in the mixing of feeds in Canada. With regard to the surplus of milk and the surplus of butter and other edible food products suitable for human consumption, they could be used as part of the school lunch program in Canada. I think our products can be disposed of. I would suggest instead of this backward looking policy of cutting prices and removing supports, this is the kind of program that should be set forth at the coming meeting in Washington when they are discussing the all-important food for peace program. Food for peace should be something of a co-operative program between nations, and this is the kind of policy that I suggest the Canadian government should advance.
It has been suggested very often, Mr. Chairman, that the sums of money the western delegates have demanded could not be provided. It has been suggested that they have asked for too much. I suggest they have not asked for too much and that they themselves have put forward ways and means by which this money can be obtained. They have come here and have said, "We want a deficiency payment that will guarantee us a certain price for wheat." They have said that to the extent they can get any part of this payment on any other basis they are prepared to reduce their demand. Implement a two-price system and you automatically reduce the deficiency payment asked for by the prairie grain growers. Take action on the exchange rate so that Canadian wheat will be selling on the basis of dollars of equal value to United States dollars. By that means you will increase the price of wheat another four or five cents a bushel. Pay from the national treasury the subsidy that is now charged to the Canadian wheat board, and therefore charged to the farmers, for wheat that is used in the production of flour for export. Extend the payments that are provided for storage at the end of the crop year to cover all grain in public storage and by that means you would add another substantial sum for the western wheat producer. I suggest that these measures would in fact reduce the deficiency payment which the farmer has been asking for by almost 50 per cent.
Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the final payment on last year's wheat crop would be announced within the course of a few weeks. I think it should have been announced long ago. I have argued in the agriculture committee and I have argued with support in years gone by that soon after the end of a crop year the inventory

should be accounted for, transferred to the next pool account and the farmer paid his money. The farmer should not have to wait month after month after month until the next crop year is almost over before announcement of the final payment is made. With worse drought conditions on the prairies at the present time than at any time since 1937-and we hope they will change-with the farmers so short of money that they felt it necessary to send a mass delegation to Ottawa, I plead with the minister to announce the final payment immediately and in announcing it to take into account the demands of prairie grain producers for deficiency payments and augment the final payment by a deficiency payment.
I have pointed out that the greater portion of the money spent under the Agricultural Stabilization Act has been spent outside the prairie provinces. I do not put that forward by way of criticism at all. It is necessary to support certain agricultural products. If support of these products means that most of the money at any given time goes to a certain part of Canada, I have no objection. But realizing that the Agricultural Stabilization Act has benefited in the main farmers and agricultural producers of central Canada I think the government and parliament would be justified in giving sympathetic consideration to the demands of the mass delegation and in taking action forthwith on those demands.

Mr. Chairman, we have just heard the usual sort of tirade, shall I say, which we get from the hon. member for Assiniboia. I regret very much the quite evident attempt he has made to try to raise sectional differences and to make out that one part of Canada is getting more benefit than another from the agricultural policies which the government is pursuing. That is absolutely not the case. As far as the application of the Agricultural Stabilization Act is concerned, every farmer in every part of Canada gets the same benefit from the legislation to the extent hat he engages in the raising of the products covered by that act.
I did not say anything different.

The hon. member made a great point of the fact that the majority of the money which has been used to purchase commodities under the stabilization act has been expended in a part of the country other than the prairie provinces. That does not mean anything. Where you happen to pick up the goods that you take off the market does not make any difference with respect to the total effect of the benefits produced for the farmers.

By picking up surplus butter, for example, we put into the pockets of Canadian farmers at least $80 million more in 1958 than they would have otherwise had. Where we picked up the extra butter for that purpose in order to take it off the market and to maintain the price of 64 cents which we maintained throughout last year does not make any difference. The attempt to try to make out that it does by saying that $5 million was spent by the stabilization board to purchase commodities in western Canada compared with $60 million odd in eastern Canada is not a valid argument at all. It does not establish in any way whatsoever what the benefit of the stabilization act has been in different parts of Canada.
The hon. member also goes on about the demand for so-called deficiency payments on western grain, which are not deficiency payments at all. What is being asked for is retroactive flat payments.
Who is quibbling now?
May I ask the minister a question?

Just a minute. The hon. member goes around the country trying to establish as a fact what is a complete myth, that we have not been assisting the western farmer and assisting him very materially since we have been in office.
Will the minister permit a question?
Sit down.

All right.

I do not ask my questions when sitting down. I have the permission of the minister to ask him a question. I appreciate it. I know he does not mind. In referring to these three main subsidies, I wonder whether he meant to say that the amount of $22 J million in prairie farm assistance is provided wholly from the national treasury. Is it not a fact that throughout the history of the legislation approximately half has been paid by the agricultural producers themselves? He does not want to.

With respect to the reduction in the support price on skim milk powder, he made the statement that support prices are being reduced and that this is contrary to everything that members of the government said in the last two election campaigns, and so on. It is not contrary to those promises at all. He seems to believe that once you establish a price you cannot do anything except raise that price. The price should never be reduced at any time. Once a support price has been set, that should be the price for eternity. If you do anything about that price, you should raise it but, under no circumstances should the price be reduced. This is not common sense, nor is it practicable. There is no country in the world which has a support price program of that nature. When the hon. member talks along those lines, he shows he either understands absolutely nothing about how a price support program works in this or any other country or he is just putting forth propaganda.
How about parity prices?

As a matter of fact, the whole principle of support prices is that they will move up and down, depending on market

Supply-Agriculture
conditions for the commodity, the supply of it and all sorts of other factors. I went into that in detail when the stabilization act was before the house last year. I made no attempt whatever to say anything except that we would vary the prices up and down as you must do under any stabilization act or support price legislation which will work.
In so far as skim milk powder is concerned, the hon. member seems to think we should keep the same price for skim milk powder. The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, as well as some other hon. members opposite, seem to be of the same opinion. They seem to believe that we should keep the same price for skim milk powder, no matter how many millions of pounds we have to store, no matter how many millions of pounds we may have to dump in the river or something like that. It has been explained time after time that skim milk powder is not a product you can store indefinitely. It becomes unusable after a certain length of time, and therefore it is not a product that can be stored by the tens of millions of pounds to await the eventual development of a market. You have to dispose of it in a fairly short space of time, otherwise it is going to go bad.
Apparently the hon. member for Assiniboia and a lot of other hon. members in the Liberal party do not care about that at all. They say, maintain the price; go ahead and pile up surpluses by the tens of millions of pounds. Last year, according to the statements put before the house yesterday, we bought something over 100 million pounds of this powder. If we take no action this coming year we will buy another 100 million pounds of it. So long as the stabilization board stands ready to buy every pound of milk powder that is produced at 15 cents a pound, when the world price for this powder is probably around seven or eight cents a pound, there is no question whatever about what will happen. We will continue to buy milk powder which we cannot possibly sell any place and which, our experience has shown, cannot even be given away. Nevertheless, the hon. member for Assiniboia would like us to sit there and continue doing this. This shows how impractical his ideas are, and how little he knows about how a price support program for agricultural products has to be operated, if it is going to operate at all.

There is one thing I will say in connection with support prices for dairy products as announced yesterday. We held discussions for several weeks with all the dairy producing groups in this country. We laid the whole situation before them in so far as the supply of skim milk powder, butter, cheese and other dairy products are concerned. We asked for their advice. We asked what they would recommend. We did not proceed with any action so far as support prices for dairy products were concerned without the fullest consultation with all the people concerned. As a result of that consultation we have come up with this program which I believe hon. members will find, in spite of what some members of the opposition are saying, is acceptable to the great majority of dairy farmers.
Just before I sit down, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank all hon. members who have taken part in this extended debate on item No. 1 of the agriculture estimates. I think we are now in the seventh day of our discussion of this item. Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to rise on this occasion during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture and to congratulate the minister on his fine administration during the past year. During this time he has come in for criticism, often unjust, both in and out of this house. However, I think we are all agreed in our respect for his administrative ability and for his interest and dedication in furthering a fair deal for those who are occupied in the various fields of agriculture.
I am sure that unlike some members in the other parties in this house those on the government side take pride in the success of the prices stabilization act. During the past year the prices stabilization act has cost the govenment something like $15 million. However, the net cost to the government of this act is no measure of the real effectiveness or usefulness of it.

There has been a great deal of talk about dairy products. Let us take butter as one example. It is estimated that if it had not been for the support price on butter and import controls the price of butter would have dropped from 64 cents to 40 cents a pound. Based on an estimate of 340 million pounds of butter produced in 1958, the stabilization act has added more than $80 million to the farmers' cash income. The cost to the treasury in reselling 70 million pounds of butter that was purchased by the board was something over $2 million. However, even if the cost were substantially larger, it would be relatively small compared to the value added to the farmers' income.
Yesterday we were privileged to receive a report of the inquiry into the distribution of railway box cars by Mr. Bracken. Mr. Bracken, as everyone knows, was a distinguished member of this house for years and was also a former premier of Manitoba. He distinguished himself as the head of the commission which inquired into the liquor laws of Manitoba, and his report on that subject has been largely implemented. I am sure that the report which he has presented to us will receive very careful and sympathetic consideration from the government, and I hope his recommendations will be implemented. It was a pleasure also to hear from the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the accounts for last year in connection with the sale of wheat are to be concluded, and in the not too distant future the board will be in a position to announce the final payment on this grain.
I should like for a moment to refer to the farm delegation that came to Ottawa recently. Before they arrived I, like many other hon. members, was rather dubious as to what their behaviour would be, but as soon as they arrived our doubts were dispelled. I am sure that all hon. members of this house and everyone in the building from the Prime Minister down to the guards of the House of Commons agree that the behaviour of the members of the farm delegation was exemplary. In fact, one guard told me as the delegation was leaving, "This was the finest group of gentlemen who have ever come to these buildings. Before leaving members of the delegation came and shook hands with us and told us how much they enjoyed their trip to Ottawa."
I was pleased to meet with the 17 delegates from Springfield and we discussed at great length the problems in agriculture with which they are being faced. I believe that one of the most significant accomplishments of this delegation was that it demonstrated to eastern Canada the position of western agriculture.

We have heard a great deal about the understanding and good relations that the eastern members displayed to this delegation. I should like to say a few words about the prairie members in this house. I might be forgiven in this respect because I am referring in large part to those who were members of this house in the two sessions of parliament before I myself became a member and I say this because I feel the western members are perhaps a little too modest to say it themselves.
I believe that a good deal of the credit for these good relations should go to the members from the prairies for the understanding which they have prompted in eastern Canada. Never before in Canadian history has there been such a unified voice speaking on behalf of the prairies and the western farmer. In the past we have had four political parties representing the prairies in this house each with a small number of members. This in itself would not have been bad had these members of the various parties joined together to produce a unified point of view from the west. However, they quibbled and quarrelled among themselves and the government of the day tended to ignore the west and paid little attention to the needs of those who live on the prairies. Today for the first time in history there is a unified front on the government side speaking forcefully for the farmer of western Canada and as a result of this great strides have been made in agriculture. It is a tribute to these western members that members from the east have supported all the agricultural legislation that has been brought in by this government and which was primarily of benefit to the west. I can say without fear of contradiction that these prairie members are continuing to work hard. It is not necessary to indulge in platitudes; you need merely look at the accomplishment of this government in agriculture to realize that these members have been working hard on behalf of the western farmers and will continue to work diligently on their behalf.
Since entering this house I have listened patiently to the profuse verbosity which is characteristic of emanations from Her Majesty's loyal opposition. I offer my condolences to the Liberal party on their annihilation on the prairies. I have observed that they have accepted this annihilation graciously. They do not make any presumption of representing or speaking for the prairies. Unlike them, however, the C.C.F. party which also met the same fate in 47 out of 48 seats has not accepted defeat graciously. The lone hon. member of that

party from the west has set himself up as the ultimate authority on prairie agriculture and seeks to discredit the rest of the prairie members.
I have listened to the tidal wave of weightless words which are often wafted across this chamber from the confines of the family compact in the corner. In the last few days especially we have often been inundated by an avalanche of insulting invective the value of which is not in keeping with the dignity of this house.
You are not supposed to read your speech. There is a rule against that.

I have no doubt as to the desire of the members of the C.C.F. party to serve this country well. However, I would suggest that they read Norman Vincent Peale's book entitled "The Power of Positive Thinking".
In the constituency of Springfield we have a large portion of the fertile Red river valley. In this and other areas as well the majority of farmers are mixed farmers with relatively small farms. More and more of recent years these farmers are engaging in the growing of potatoes. It was therefore with particular pleasure that we welcomed the announcement in the budget of the extension of the duty of 37J cents on United States potatoes on a year-round basis. I have advocated this measure for some time and indeed made reference to it in my maiden speech.
Previously the Canadian duty on United States potatoes was 37J cents per hundred pounds from the period June 15 to July 31 while new potatoes were allowed entry free from August 1 to June 14. Potatoes were one of the products on which the tariff board recommended the duty should be placed for the full twelve months of the year and I understand that this was one of the items which was negotiated with the United States authorities when discussions were held regarding fruit and vegetable tariffs.
Considering the crop year as being from July 1 to June 30, the five-year average figure for imports and exports for the period 1953 to 1958 is pretty well in balance, being
1,979,000	hundredweight for imports and L,937,000 hundredweight for exports. While ;he five-year average is pretty well in balance there is a marked variation from year to year. For example, while in 1954-55 we exported only 985,000 hundredweight to the United States, we imported 2,907,000 hundredweight from that country. In 1957-58, on the other hand, we exported 3,325,000 hundredweight to the United States and imported 1,523,000 hundredweight from that country.

The situation in the current crop year was of concern to the producers of Manitoba. Their concern can be appreciated if we compare wholesale potato prices at Winnipeg on the basis of a 75 pound bag. As shown in the March issue of "The current review of agricultural conditions in Canada", issued by the federal Department of Agriculture, the Winnipeg local price for Canadian No. 1 potatoes was as follows:

While I am quoting wholesale prices may I say that the price to the producer is substantially lower. The spread in price from producer to consumer is another matter of concern to the farmer. Potato prices this year are substantially lower than those of a year ago, but it was not only the price that caused concern. The inability of the producer to market his product was of great concern to the potato grower, too.
The large United States surplus of potatoes this year caused depressed prices to Canadian producers. On December 26, 1958 United States imports forced Manitoba potato prices down to $1.10 for a 75 pound bag as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of that date. The article went on to say that a provincial department of agriculture spokesman said he believed a price of $1.50 would give a return to the producer which would bear a fair relationship to production costs. As reported in the article he went on to state:
However, the low shipping charges from the potato-producing areas of Minnesota and North Dakota influence Manitoba prices. Over-production in these areas can force our retail prices down to levels below the cost of production.
During the current marketing season imports have been markedly higher than in 1957-58. From July 1 to November 30, 1958 imports from the United States totalled
586,000	hundredweight compared with 489,000 hundredweight a year earlier. Three hundred and sixty-nine thousand hundredweight of potatoes were imported into western Canada in that period, an increase of 44 per cent over the year previous. Canadian exports of table and seed potatoes from July 1, 1958 to February 20, 1959 totalled 1.7 million hundredweight compared with 2.7 million hundredweight exported during the same period a year earlier. Almost all the decrease was accounted for by reduced shipments to the United States. February 1 stocks of potatoes in the central United States were 52 per cent higher than the year earlier. Total United States stocks, in spite of unusually large disappearance, were 16 per cent higher.

In Canada holdings of potatoes on March 1, 1959 amounted to 9.1 million hundredweight. This was 16 per cent less than they were the year earlier, and in spite of the lower stocks in Canada, as a result of the heavy United States surplus, prices in western Canada began the season lower than in 1957 and have held steadily lower in the 1958-59 marketing period. It was therefore encouraging that the government took this measure to discourage the dumping of United States potatoes into Canada, because the United States farmer enjoys somewhat more favourable conditions of production.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance for the initiative they have shown in bringing in this duty which will tend to make marketing conditions more favourable to domestic growers. At the same time I am sure it is not going to affect the price to the consumer to any extent because of the wide spread between what the producer receives and what the consumer pays. But what it will do is to provide an expanded market for domestically grown potatoes. I would recommend that because of this wide spread perhaps some further measures be taken to give the producer a price which will bear a fair relationship to what the consumer pays, and which bears a fair relationship to his costs of production.

The board shall from time to time in accordance with this act take such action as is necessary to stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities at their respective prescribed prices, and shall take such action and make such recommendations as are necessary to ensure that the prescribed prices for an agricultural commodity in effect from time to time shall bear a fair relationship to the cost of production of such commodity.

I am glad to see this change.

I knew the hon. gentleman would be happy, and I am trying to accommodate him as far as I can, consistent with my obligations, in pointing out the many errors into which he has been plunged by the character of his own policy

and his failure, sometimes, to realize that there has been a gap between the declaration of that policy and its actual achievement.

You are quite wrong.

I point out that if this price he is talking about were put into effect the taxpayers, in other words, through the deficiency payments which would have to be made, would be paying about half of the

price, between 40 and 50 per cent of the price that the soybean producers would be getting which, I think, he would agree is not a reasonable proportion.

I say I would want to see all of the facts. What I am doing now is putting forward the case put forward by the soybean growers themselves. I am a little disturbed from what the minister has said about the effect of his declaration with regard to the existing floor price of $2.10 which no one certainly can, in the face of all the circumstances, regard as unfair in the situation.
Then the minister has before the board a request with regard to the sugar beet growers.
I ask the minister to take all these things into consideration when he comes to develop his policy for this year with regard to these matters.
I have had letters of thanks from the sugar beet people on the support price put in last year.

I think my hon. friend deserves the thanks, but I am not talking about last year. I am now talking about this year. I will tell him that he will get a letter of thanks from me if he listens to the representations which I am making.
It would be the first one.

No; I have written to my hon. friend many times. If I did not have occasion to thank him on many occasions it is simply because he did not deserve thanks; but I assure him that if he does listen to my recommendations he will receive my full gratitude.
Before I take my seat I should like to say this. I know the minister is faced with criticisms from this side of the house. The reason for those criticisms rests on the doorstep of hon. gentlemen opposite who for years in this house told the farmers of Canada that the existing agricultural policy was not satisfactory; that the farmers of Canada were not sharing adequately in the income of the nation, and that the only way to rectify this situation was to put hon. gentlemen opposite in power. Hon. gentlemen opposite are now in power and if there are marches on Ottawa and if there are marches to be created in order to assess the effect of the first march; if groups from farm organizations continued to come to Ottawa complaining about the gap between accomplishment and promises, the responsibility lies only on the shoulders of the Prime Minister and members of the government who talked about parity and about deficiency payments in such a way as to give the farmers of this country the feeling that

under this government, with its formula, farmers could look for substantial economic improvement in the lot of agriculture. That is the situation. If the Minister of Agriculture would some day, or perhaps in the course of these estimates, simply rise and say: Well, we promised too much; our promises were extravagant; we are now in power and we see that the situation is not what we thought; we now realize that the last government really did do something for the farmers of Canada; if he would take that kind of attitude he would find that his estimates would pass quickly and that he would have less trouble than his continuous and persistent championing of a case that is so obviously faulty and so obviously invalid.

I do want to say a few words on this item; I think it is the appropriate one. In the Kootenays we have a climate and soil that are ideal for the growing of cherries. Our cherries are of first-class quality. This has been recognized by western Canada, in some parts of the United States and even by prominent fruit people in Great Britain. Nevertheless, our production and quality of cherries have been affected in recent years by a disease known as "little cherry" and a disease known as "brown rot". These diseases have affected the production of cherries particularly in certain areas and they have had a serious effect on replanting because, so far as little cherry disease is concerned, a satisfactory solution has not been found to the problem. I am sure the minister knows what I am talking about because he comes to Kootenay West on occasion for summer holidays and knows some of the orchards I am talking about. I want to read briefly from the report of the royal commission on the tree fruit industry of British Columbia prepared by Dean E. D. MacPhee. I will do so briefly and it will 66968-9-193i
Supply-Agriculture
save speaking at length. He has this to say with respect to little cherry on page 188:
One of the two serious blows to the cherry industry in the Kootenay area was the "little cherry" virus. This disease was first discovered in 1933, but it was not recognized as a virus disease. In 1934, three of the orchards near the point of the original outbreak were showing "little cherry."
I know those orchards quite well.
By 1940 the disease had spread in an area 20 miles in diameter. It was in 1940 that Mr. W. R. Foster, assistant plant pathologist with the British Columbia department of agriculture, was delegated to study this disease, and in 1941 he determined the cause to be a virus. By 1947 it was found that all of the cherry areas of the Kootenays, except the Deer Park-Renata area, were showing the virus.
That is not quite correct because on my own ranch, which is very limited in area, there is no little cherry disease as yet.
This rapid spread of "little cherry" in the Kootenays took place in spite of many natural barriers, such as mountain ranges, large lakes, and often considerable distances between orchards.
In 1946 the federal government set up a sublaboratory at Creston to study this disease, and these investigations are continuing. Studies have been carried out to determine how the disease is spread, and it is reasonably well established that insects are the carriers of the virus.
I will not read any more but I want to bring this serious question to the attention of the minister again. Before proceeding, I wish to pay tribute to the work done by the officials of the department, particularly the research workers at the Summerland experimental station. However in my opinion you cannot carry on an adequate investigation unless you have sufficient funds. In view of the importance of this industry to the Kootenays, a district particularly well suited for the production of cherries, pears and peaches in some areas, I am asking for a more intensive study of the question so that an economic solution can be found in order that many of our young people will again have faith in planting young cherry orchards which will no doubt produce such fruit as has made the district famous in the past.
There is a general feeling among the cherry growers in our district that the matter has been treated in a sort of piecemeal and timid manner. I bring it to the attention of the minister again, present the views of those persons interested in the re-development of the cherry industry in the Kootenays and urge a full scale attack upon the problem.
The second one is brown rot, a serious disease which we have had for a good number of years. I read again from page 189 of the same report in order to condense my remarks:
Brown-rot is the second serious disease in the Kootenay area. Brown-rot has been known in the

Supply-Agriculture
Kootenay area for many decades. The severity of this disease is directly correlated with the degree of summer moisture and the amount of attention growers give their orchards. Unfortunately, since the late forties and during the fifties, there have been a number of cool wet summers, which have caused this disease to develop into epidemic proportions, especially in semi-neglected orchards.
Brown-rot is a disease which is spread by a fungus, the spore of which live over winter for the most part in an infected fruit which has fallen to the ground. These infected fruits are called "mummies''. The disease can also be carried over on infected twigs and spurs. The first infection period occurs in the spring from the pink stage of cherry through to the fall of the husk. This period is extremely critical, and it is imperative that developing growth be covered with a protective film of fungicide. Mr. J. E. Swales, district horticulturist for the Kootenay area, points out that from the experience gained in 1957 sprays should be applied at intervals not longer than four days during the blossom period, regardless of weather conditions.
I want to bring to the minister's attention that this disease has been prevalent for many years in the southeastern portion of British Columbia and I believe it has caused serious concern to cherry growers in some sections of eastern Canada, in portions of the United States at times and also in Europe. I have read quite a lot of the literature on the question. Because the disease was not serious in extent until recent years there was no work done by the minister's department with respect to testing in orchards and research of that sort. During the past year control measures have been studied in the Deer Park-Renata area with a considerable degree of success as a result of the co-operation of the personnel from the department and the growers concerned.
In the first place, these investigations should have been carried on before. It was not good enough to allow this disease to reach epidemic proportions under circumstances which are bound to recur in certain seasons, that is, with an excessive amount of rain, hot weather and consequent relative humidity. These are the conditions that produce the spores which produce the brown rot disease.
During the last two or three seasons we have had these conditions in our district during cherry growing and cherry picking times and very large losses have resulted from brown rot. Brown rot is a very insidious disease. You can pick fruit that appears to be in first-class condition, pack it, place it in a reefer car, and before it reaches the Calgary market the crates of cherries will in some cases be covered with a white mould or rot will have developed on the under layers of the cherries in the pack.
I mention this to the minister because it is a very important thing to our growers. I
[Mr. Herridge.l
do ask for an extension of the control measures into other orchards and other areas of the district. I ask that the minister's department seek the co-operation of the growers in these control measures and studies to the advantage of the growers concerned at the present time and the long term advantage of the industry and therefore the district.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon.
member for Kootenay West says, I have indeed enjoyed the scenery and the fruit in the interior of British Columbia in the days when I used to be able to take a summer holiday. I hope that the balance of the session will proceed in such a way that that will be possible again this year. In connection with little cherry, the hon. member has brought this matter to the attention of the government on various occasions for many years past. I can remember him speaking on it on several occasions. I should like to assure him that we are continuing research on the disease at Summerland and also, I believe, at the station we now have at Creston. How much success is being achieved in finding a means of controlling the disease I am sorry I am not able to tell him without having the matter looked up. I have not the information with me at the present time. However, I should like to assure him that we will continue research into the disease with the hope that something will be found which will control it or bring it to an end.
As far as brown rot is concerned, a spray has been developed consisting of sulphur and d.d.t., I believe, which, if applied twice during the period the trees are blossoming, does control brown rot fairly well. Research is still going on at Summerland in connection with brown rot in an attempt to find a better means of either controlling it or stamping it out.

I thank the minister for his remarks and I rise again just to say that I overlooked one point I intended to mention when I was speaking before. I think the officials of the department are inclined to hide their light under a bushel. For instance, I found that in the district of Renata, which I know very weR, there were a number of cherry growers who were having considerable success in their co-operation with the officials in connection with the sprays the minister has just mentioned. However, when I went to Edgewood, they seemed to have no knowledge of exactly what was happening in the other places. I suggest it would be a good idea if the department issued periodical releases through the local press concerning

what is happening with respect to the cooperative studies on brown rot and the progress being made with the studies on little cherry disease. I think this would be helpful.

I thoroughly agree with the hon. member that the result of the research should be put into the hands of the people who can make use of it as rapidly as possible and by the most effective possible means. As the hon. member knows, there is an extension program, I think it is called, by means of which the results of this work are put into the hands of the farmers. This program is primarily one of the things carried on by the province. We do the research and we turn the results of that over to the provincial departments of agriculture and other bodies. By and large they put it into the hands of the people who can make use of it.
In the Okanagan valley there is a joint committee of the provincial department and our own department which attempts to get the results of our research out as rapidly and as effectively as possible. I am sorry to hear that the knowledge of this spray for brown rot apparently did not get to certain cherry growers, and also I presume peach and plumb growers, because those are the three types of trees affected. I would hope that co-operation between the dominion and provincial officials, and the community as a whole, would be such that we would not have lags of this kind.
The information did reach them, but too late for them to take advantage of it during the growing season.

10. Agricultural Stabilization Act administration, $103,710.

In rising to take part in this debate on item 10 of the agriculture estimates, which deals with the Agricultural Stabilization Act, I should like to say that this legislation, which was desired by the farmers across Canada and has been in operation for only one year has proven to be excellent legislation. It is regrettable, however, that wheat, oats and barley, being under the jurisdiction of the wheat board now, could not be brought under this stabilization act. All other agricultural commodities are either under the act or could be brought under the act, but our most important products such as wheat, oats and barley are outside the scope of the stabilization act.
I am not prepared to suggest what steps should be taken to bring these grains under the protection of the stabilization act, but as a long range step toward stabilizing prices
Supply-Agriculture
for western grains a method should be found. There are some other agricultural products that are not under the stabilization act right now which should be brought under it, and I refer particularly to rapeseed. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to give a short history of rapeseed growing in the west.
The growing of rapeseed in Canada on a large scale commenced in 1943. At that time the British, Canadian and United States navies needed supplies of rapeseed oil to be used as marine oil. The Canadian wheat board purchased all rapeseed from the growers during that period at a guaranteed price of six cents per pound. After the war the wheat board discontinued the purchase of rapeseed, and as a result of this the price dropped sharply from a high of six cents per pound to a low of 2.3 cents per pound last year. In 1957, as a result of the heavy wheat surplus, more rapeseed was produced and, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, 629,000 acres were seeded to rapeseed, of which 535,000 acres were in Saskatchewan alone. The output of rape-seed in 1942 was 420,000 pounds, but by 1957 it had increased to 423 million pounds. As I have said, last year the price dropped to a low of 2.3 cents per pound, the lowest price we ever received in the history of the industry. It is for this reason I am requesting that rapeseed should be brought under the stabilization act in order to keep prices in line instead of having them drop to a level that will destroy the producer.
We have no rapeseed surplus as yet, and the way rapeseed oil is being utilized much more could be produced. I have with me a clipping from a newspaper which states that the opportunities for vegetable oil crops are tremendous. It reads:
Opportunities for expansion of Canadian vegetable oil seed crops were described as "fantastic" and "tremendous" by a spokesman for the edible oil foods industry.
Robin E. Merry, president of the institute of edible oil foods, speaking at the institute's fifth annual meeting said that within six years Canada will need a billion pounds of foods fats and oil annually to meet the needs of its growing population...
Unless the increase in Canadian needs of vegetable oils is to continue to be supplied by even greater imports, an all-out program to assist Canadian farmers to convert to soybean and other vegetable oil seed farming must begin at once, said Mr. Merry...
"We can no longer afford the luxury of obsolete thinking about farming," he said. "Federal and provincial governments appear to be guilty of such thinking and seem to be unaware of the need for positive programs designed to help farmers seize the opportunity for profitable vegetable oil seed farming."

S upply-A gricu Iture
This, Mr. Chairman, is the reason I am asking that rapeseed be brought under the stabilization act. As the member for the Humboldt-Melfort constituency I am aware of the fact that half of the rapeseed grown in Saskatchewan is grown in my constituency. I cannot stand idly by and see the rapeseed industry, which is so vital to the Canadian economy, receive less than fair treatment from our Minister of Agriculture.
I should like to bring this to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as well. The fact that rapeseed was grown on acres that would have been otherwise seeded to wheat meant that we were able to reduce the wheat surplus by millions of bushels. Credit must be given to our Minister of Trade and Commerce for making such a creditable attempt to cut the wheat surplus. Unless rapeseed is brought under the stabilization act, thereby giving the growers a fair chance to get a good price, these acres will again be put into wheat, thus increasing our wheat surplus. The only hope the rapeseed producers have at the present time is that parliament will act to bring rapeseed under the stabilization act and thus give the industry a square deal.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to the matter of wheat, oats and barley produced in western Canada for the wheat board not being under the stabilization act, which the hon. member mentioned, may I point out that no doubt the hon. gentleman knows this is due to the fact that it is handled by another government board, the wheat board. When the stabilization act was being prepared the wheat pools in western Canada asked that western wheat, oats and barley not be placed under the stabilization act but remain under the wheat board. I think it is certainly wise not to attempt to handle these commodities simultaneously through two government boards.
As far as rapeseed is concerned this is the first request I have ever received to have this commodity placed under the stabilization act. There has been no request up to date, to my knowledge, from any of the producers of rapeseed to the effect that it should be placed under price support. If there are requests of that kind the stabilization board and advisory committee will consider them but again I state we have received none to date.
The request made by the hon. member that rapeseed be placed under this act and his remarks concerning the possibility of producing sufficient rapeseed in Canada to meet Canada's vegetable oil requirements point up again some of the difficulties that are encountered in these matters. We had a recent

request by the hon. member for Essex East that soybeans be given a high support price this year. Several other hon. gentlemen mentioned soybeans and the fact that we do not produce nearly as many as we could produce and that the demand for vegetable oil in Canada is larger than our total production of soybeans. It must be remembered that rapeseed oil, sunflower seed oil, flax seed oil and various other oils all interact in terms of production. We could have in Canada a larger production of vegetable oil than we could possibly consume in the country. I just mention this to illustrate the fact that there is a danger in overproduction. The fact that we import a certain amount of soybean oil each year does not indicate that we should proceed to expand our soybean production more or less indefinitely. The same thing applies to rapeseed production or the production of any other oil producing crop. We must look at the picture as a whole and take into consideration the fact that if we expanded production of any of these crops to the extent that expansion could take place in Canada we would meet the entire market and it would make it difficult as far as the production of similar crops is concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I directed a question this morning to the Minister of Agriculture to which I have not had a reply. I asked the minister what would be the price for skim powdered milk, roller processed.
The price for roller processed dried skim milk will be proportionately the same as for the spray processed commodity. It will be two cents under-that is, eight cents-for the roller processed product.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say on this item. I trust it is the appropriate one on which to mention the question of the marketing of tree fruits. As the minister knows, marketing is the principal problem of tree fruit growers as it is with nearly all agricultural producers.
In British Columbia there has been a great deal done with respect to self help on the part of the growers and their efforts to obtain satisfactory legislation. As a result of years of effort the British Columbia marketing act was brought into being under which we have the tree fruit board. Working under the act and under this board is the organization called Tree Fruits Limited which is the growers' sales agency. Owing to the particular problems that have arisen in recent years with respect to the marketing of tree fruits in general, and particularly apples, there is a growing realization among fruit growers in British Columbia that the problem cannot be met on a provincial basis alone

and that it is going to take co-operation within the industry throughout Canada if they are going to market their fruits to the best advantage under any given set of circumstances.
That feeling has been growing for a number of years and it found expression in the last convention of the British Columbia fruit growers' association which was held in Vernon from January 20 to January 22, 1959. That expression was highlighted by the adoption of two resolutions which I want to place on the record because to me and to those persons who have been interested in the tree fruit industry for a number of years they represent a progressive step in the thinking of the persons who have had particularly to do with these problems.
The first resolution that was considered by the convention was a resolution entitled "Cooperation amongst fruit producing areas" which was introduced by the Penticton delegation. They are quite a progressive lot down in Penticton; they come second only to those in the Kootenays. This resolution reads as follows:
Whereas the conquest of the moon has become a real and serious objective of apparently responsible governments, while at the same time the very existence and welfare of those who produce man's food on this planet-notably that of the fruit grower -appear to be of minor concern to those not directly affected, and
Whereas the only effective remedy for the growers' plight must be self help through extended co-operation,
Therefore be it resolved by this 1959 B.C.F.G.A. convention that their governing bodies be instructed to take definite and vigorous steps to bring about such co-operation among the major fruit producing areas of this northern continent that eventually all futile and destructive cut-throat competition may become a thing of the past, and be superseded by some form of orderly marketing such as this organization has demonstrated is feasible among the growers of this province.
To illustrate the comprehensive approach which is developing, I might mention that an amendment was moved to this resolution urging that the words "this northern continent" be deleted and that the word "Canada" be substituted therefor. When that amendment was placed before the convention it was defeated which indicates that the growers realize that not only must we co-operate within the province or within the country in the marketing of agricultural commodities but we have to have some degree of cooperation with the growers in other countries. I believe this is a very forward step.
After that resolution was unanimously adopted, as I understand it, the convention then discussed the next step with respect to what would flow from this co-operation between tree fruit growers in Canada. The
Supply-Agriculture
convention then passed the following resolution which was put forward by the south and east Kelowna delegation and entitled "Canadian fruit board". It reads as follows:
Whereas the average return for apples for the 1957 crop, even with the deficiency payment, was inadequate to meet the cost of production, and Whereas our own organization has done all in its power to secure the highest possible returns to the grower but has not been able to do so, not for lack of effort, but due to controlling only one-third of Canada's production in a small contained area, Therefore be it resolved by this 1959 B.C.F.G.A. convention that we work primarily through the Canadian Horticultural Council to obtain the two things absolutely essential for the economic stability of this industry, and they are:
1.	The establishment of a Canadian fruit board to handle the entire national and international selling of our fruit, and
2.	A minimum price for our fruit commensurate with the cost of production.
I am particularly interested in the change in thinking that has occurred over the years. Until recent years I was closely associated with the British Columbia fruit growers' association and attended a number of conventions. At one time it was extremely difficult to get any consideration for a national approach to this problem. At that time growers tended to depend on the high quality of the fruit, the fruit packing and the advantage they would receive in competition with some other area in that respect. They found out as a result of experience that regardless of what is done to improve the pack or the efficiency of the organization in general, to meet with success they must co-operate with other fruit growing districts in Canada and with those in the United States to the south of us. They recommend the establishment of a Canadian fruit board. I do urge the minister to give consideration to this new expression of opinion on the part of the British Columbia fruit growers, and I ask that serious study be commenced by the appropriate officials of the minister's department of legislation suitable to meet the particular, and in some way the peculiar needs of the fruit industry in Canada, to the end we establish a Canadian fruit board in due time.

I am glad, Mr. Chairman, that the fruit growers of British Columbia have passed a resolution to put forward their representations, and take action through the Canadian Horticultural Council. We have been encouraging horticulturalists right across Canada to do that ever since I have been in this position in order to get away from the business of regional representations which are often in direct conflict with each other, because they are made by every small section of the country. I found not very long after I became Minister of Agriculture that,

Supply-Agriculture
for example, the fruit growers of a particular kind in British Columbia wanted action which was diametrically opposed to the action which was being requested at the same time by the growers of that same kind of fruit in Ontario. This seemed to me to be the sort of situation which the fruit growers should thrash out amongst themselves, and therefore we have been trying to encourage them to take these matters up in the horticultural council and come to some agreement amongst themselves before they come to us asking for action. I am glad that the British Columbia fruit growers apparently have adopted a resolution to follow that practice.
So am I.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if we could have some further clarification from the minister as to what policy the government is going to follow as far as the support price of hogs is concerned. I am wondering if any result has yet been obtained from the study which is going on as to whether the deficiency payment, if it is inaugurated after October 1, will be limited-and I understand that is the thinking of the department and the minister-and what the ceiling may be on the number of hogs on which a deficiency payment may be made. The minister may say that this has not yet been determined, and if that is the situation I hope he will consider very carefully keeping the ceiling at a reasonably high level. I do not think the number of hogs on which a deficiency payment may be made should be so low as to encourage inefficient production or very small farms. I am enthusiastically in favour of removing support prices from great corporations or very large industries engaged in the production of hogs. If vertical integration in the production of hogs is extended, I think the formula outlined by the minister is one way by which it may be discouraged. But I think that in setting the ceiling as to the number of hogs eligible for deficiency payments, the number per farmer should be such as to enable an efficient farmer to make a reasonably good living in the production of hogs. It should not be a system of rationing the production of hogs or a system which will lend itself to a very small quota or number per farm being eligible.
When the minister is replying I wonder if he would comment on the quantity of pork products now held by the board and state whether he feels this is a very large quantity, and how it compares with quantities held by the board in previous years? Would he say whether the surpluses or quantities held by the board are the main reason that the government is considering this new kind of policy to which he referred some weeks ago? 
I would like some information as to what the plans of the board may be to dispose of this surplus pork, how it will be worked on the market, and in particular whether the quantity now held by the board will be placed on the Canadian market after the time when support prices are removed and in their place put the support price based on a deficiency technique.

Mr. Chairman, as far as the general scheme is concerned I thought I had made that relatively clear in my statement and in my answer to one or two questions in the house afterwards. In any event, the idea is to maintain the support price by means of deficiency payments. I should like to emphasize this point. There seems still to be considerable confusion in some newspaper articles I have read between a support price as opposed to, as represented in these newspaper articles, a deficiency payment, as though they were completely different things. This is not the situation. A deficiency payment is a method of maintaining a support price, and a support price and a deficiency payment are not completely different things, as a considerable number of newspaper writers whose articles I have read in recent weeks seem to indicate.
I have said here several times that we establish a support price. That is the price which the farmer will receive for his product. We ensure he receives that price either by purchasing the product at that price or we give him the difference between the price he actually gets for the product sold on the open market and the support price we have established. We give him that difference by means of a deficiency payment. We can do it in some cases by certain other methods, such as the type of method the western grain farmers asked for, the retroactive flat payment. There are various other methods; but in any event the policy, as soon as it is worked out, will be to maintain the support price which has been announced for the first six months, which is now $25 per hundred pounds basis Montreal and Toronto markets, and for the following six months, $23.65 per hundred pounds basis those same markets, with appropriate differentials on other markets. The hon. member seemed to think we were going to change the method of support from purchasing the article, as we are doing at the present time, to the deficiency payment method when the price change goes into effect. That is not the case. We are going to put this deficiency payment method of supporting a price into effect just as soon as we can assemble the necessary information to determine what number of hogs we should support

and have worked out the general administrative changes which will be necessary in order to carry this into effect.
In other words, we do not intend to wait until the end of September before putting this into effect. We shall put this into effect in a month, if we can get the necessary information and can get the administrative machinery set up in that time. I am not saying it will be a month; I expect it will be more like two or three months. In any event I believe it will be before the end of September.
As far as the ceiling on the number of hogs is concerned this is one of the matters with respect to which we require information. I do not know what the ceiling will be and I do not intend to guess at it. One thing I might say in connection with it, is this: the suggestions I receive depend entirely, it would seem, on the number of hogs that the man making the suggestion raises. I have had all kinds of suggestions already, ranging all the way from 50 hogs up to several hundred. Thus, I cannot answer that part of the question now, except to say that the ceiling would be set at a point which I hope will make it possible for the largest number of farmers possible to be able to make a reasonable living out of hog raising.
As a main industry?

In some cases, yes. In any event, the only reason we are putting a ceiling on the number of hogs a farmer can deliver is to prevent contract farmers from beating the system. We could just cut out contracts and integrated operations which we know exist and pay the deficiency payments to the other farmers, but if we attempted to do that nothing would be accomplished because all that would happen would be that the hogs would be delivered in different peoples names under contracts of different sizes. So in order to have any control, some limit has to be imposed on everyone. This is really a control measure. It is the only way in which a scheme of this sort could, in practice, be put into effect and accomplish the purpose which we have in mind.
As to the manner in which the pork presently on hand is to be disposed of, I may say that we hope to sell some of it on the Canadian market as the price rises, as I think it undoubtedly will. In other words, if we hold this pork for a certain length of time we expect we will find a market for it. We do not, of course, intend to break the market as the hon. member has suggested. That is one thing we certainly do not wish to do. In addition, I think we have some chance of selling some of this pork abroad. That was
Supply-Agriculture
one of the reasons I went overseas, last fall, to investigate the possibilities of opening up markets again for our pork in Britain and in other European countries. I think we shall be able to sell some pork in Britain and in Europe during the coming year. I cannot say definitely that we shall be able to do so, but I think there is a fair chance of this happening.
