Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks about the poultry industry in Canada, and particularly, in the province of Quebec. The poultry industry in Quebec is faced with some very difficult problems, mostly in the production of broilers. Last year, and especially last fall, broilers sold for 14 to 16 cents a pound; today, the price is about 17 cents a pound. Now, it is a known fact that it costs about 21 cents to the most efficient producers to produce one pound of broiler, while the cost can run as high as 29 cents for the average producer.
Would the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) consider the opportunity of establishing a deficiency price for poultry meat, and more particularly for broiler meat? I believe that the farmers have made representations on that matter to the minister last fall, besides asking him to reduce the number of export permits for poultry.

If I may say a word with regard to this question of putting price supports under poultry, particularly broiler chicks in which, I think, the hon. member is particularly interested, I would point out that this is just not a practical possibility. I do not look upon the production of these broilers as a real farm operation, because it is really a factory operation. It does not require a farm. It does not require even a rural atmosphere. It can be carried on in the middle of a city. A man puts up a building, buys several thousand chicks and then feeds them up to three and a half pounds or so. Along those lines he can turn out birds by the thousand every week. It is not a farm operation at all; it is a production line operation, and because practically no ground is required it is the type of operation which can lead to almost unlimited production.
If there were a guaranteed price for broiler chickens in effect in this country there could be produced here ten times as many broiler chickens as we in Canada could possibly eat and, of course, as the hon. member knows,

speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. Broome (Vancouver South) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING FILING OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-22, to amend the Companies Act.
He said: Before I go into the details of this bill and the intent behind it, I do wish to point out to hon. members who may disagree with some of the wording that the Companies Act is a very involved act and it is rather difficult for a private member, with the limited resources at his disposal, to bring in a properly worded bill. However, since this is simply second reading, which means approval in principle, I feel that the various legal problems involved can well be dealt with in committee. This is particularly pertinent because there have been no amendments to the Companies Act since 1934, and conditions have changed rather remarkably since 1934.
The purpose of the bill, as shown in the explanatory note, is to prevent public companies taking advantage of the exemption given in section 121 of the Companies Act to private companies-among other requirements, those not having more than 50 shareholders-by which the so-called "family" companies do not have to file annual statements with the Secretary of State. Under the present definitions and section 121 large companies are able to avoid filing annual financial statements by incorporating private companies and becoming shareholders therein.

The Canadian Companies Act, as it now stands, is taken almost word for word from the English companies act, but in 1948 the English companies act was revised and a provision was inserted in that act to cover the point I am trying to cover in this bill.
Generally speaking, there are a lot of other sections in the Companies Act that need revision. It would not hurt it if the Companies Act had a thorough going over.
The intent of the bill is two-fold. First, under the present law a public company, that is a company with more than 50 shareholders, can purchase a private company and operate that private company and in the operation of that private company, although they are forced to divulge facts in regard to the operation of the public company, under the law they do not have to divulge any details in regard to its operation.
This might well be exemplified by a communication which all hon. members received from a gentleman containing an excerpt from the Toronto Star of Friday, April 10, 1959 which details certain happenings at the annual meeting of the Canadian General Electric Company. One of the few Canadian shareholders tried to inquire into the activities of the private companies owned by the public company, Canadian General Electric, and he was unable to get the information he wanted.
I would think it should be rather axiomatic that any law laid down by a government should have for its purpose not only the protection of majority stockholders in a company but, far more important, the protection of the interests of minority shareholders. Under the present Companies Act this just is not so. The majority shareholders can, if they are not receiving the information they want, elect a new board of directors but the minority shareholders are utterly powerless. Actually in one respect the bill does not go far enough because minority shareholders of private companies today have to pay in order to receive financial statements. One of the definitions of a private company is that it shall have not more than 50 shareholders. The expense of printing such statements is not great and minority shareholders should receive these statements as a matter of right.
Although, as I say, that is one purpose of the bill, perhaps the other purpose is of much more public interest, namely the hiding behind the private companies' section of the Companies Act of large corporations which are essentially not private companies but rather public companies. In this respect the problem is to decide in what sense the property of a large business is private and, if it is private, who is entitled to such 66968-9-194J
Companies Act
privacy. Under our present regulations, as I said before, the criterion has been the number of shareholders. In other days that was an indication of the size of the company but that is not so today. In this era of large international corporations with extensive holdings in many countries the criterion of the number of shareholders does not hold good with these wholly owned subsidiaries because the stock of the subsidiary is voted through the directors of the parent corporation. They therefore qualify as to number of shareholders but this is simply begging the question because in all other respects they are properly public companies.
In dealing with the questions of foreign investment in Canada the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects made three recommendations, with the second of which the bill is concerned. The three recommendations are found on page 393 of their report and read as follows:
1.	Wherever possible, such concerns-
The reference is to foreign subsidiaries.
-should employ Canadians in senior management and technical positions, should retain Canadian engineering and other professional and service personnel, and should do their purchasing of supplies, materials and equipment in this country.
2.	They should publish their financial statements and make full disclosure of the results of their Canadian operations.
3.	They should include on their boards of directors a number of independent Canadians and they should sell an appreciable interest in their equity stock to Canadians.
Mention is made of 20 to 25 per cent. In dealing specifically with their second recommendation they had this to say, as found on page 394 of the final report of the commission:
The second objective is that foreign-owned concerns should publish or make available their financial statements showing the results of their operations in Canada. If these concerns, more particularly the larger ones, were owned in Canada, they would be required to supply copies of their financial statements to Canadian shareholders and in this way, if there were more than just a few shareholders, these statements would be made public. Generally speaking the parent concerns publish their own statements in considerable detail in their own countries.
I might add that the requirements with regard to the publication of such statements in the United States, for instance, compared with the requirements in Canada are much more extensive. They require a greater degree of disclosure of company operations and in many respects they are far ahead of what we require under our Companies Act. The commissioners go on to say:
It is not unreasonable therefore that Canadians should wish similar information about the activities of the subsidiaries in this country. Indeed, it is our opinion that the community at large is entitled to

Companies Act
be interested in the financial results of the operations of the larger foreign-owned concerns operating in this country, since in many cases these operations have a direct bearing upon economic activity and the level of employment. We do not propose that foreign-owned concerns operating in Canada should be forced to publish their financial statements-
By that they mean the taking of advertisements in newspapers in order to acquaint the public in that manner.
-but we believe it might well be in their best interests to do so voluntarily. Such a step should improve the public relations of such concerns and should allay unjustified suspicions about their operations and activities in Canada.
With regard to the extent of the operations of such subsidiaries, I wish to quote a statement taken from an article by Professor J. E. Smyth, published in the Queen's Quarterly, the autumn issue of 1958, which statement reads as follows:
Until about four years ago the Bank of Canada compiled and published financial data from a sample of Canadian companies; it has since abandoned the series. One of the important limitations of these data was that they were drawn entirely from published financial statements, and that the proportion of Canadian economic activity which was affected by large private companies, for which no statements were available, was so significant as to invalidate any conclusions which might be drawn from the published figures.
If any hon. members are in doubt as to the degree of this control of Canadian industry I should like to read a few percentage figures from the book, "Canada-United States Economic Relations" issued by the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. In this regard I am referring to the degree of control and not the degree of 100 per cent ownership. With regard to automobiles and parts, the percentage of that industry controlled by United States residents is 95 per cent and in the case of rubber 84 per cent. No figure is available for electrical apparatus but the figure as to the amount owned is 62 per cent, and the figure for the amount controlled should be similar. In chemicals the figure is 51 per cent; for the petroleum industry 68 per cent; other mining 54 per cent; pulp and paper 45 per cent; smelting and refining of non-ferrous native ores, 55 per cent; all other manufacturing 43 per cent. This table is found on page 104 of the book to which I referred.
Considering these facts it is rather interesting that so often you hear the statement made that labour unions should be forced by law to publish financial statements for the information of their members and the public at large, and the commonly used argument is that the financial affairs of companies and

businesses are open to public knowledge and that if this is fair for companies it should also be fair for unions.
Without taking sides pro or con all I wish to say is that what I have said so far should clearly indicate that it is not true that the business affairs of a very large section of Canadian business are open to the public. This goes even a little bit farther, in that it confers on the so-called private companies an advantage over public companies. The statements of operations of public companies are open to their competitors, but the private companies' affairs are secret. For instance, if you take a sampling of industry you will find that the statements of the Ford motor company are available to all the people of Canada, but those of General Motors and Chrysler are not. If you want to look at the pulp and paper industry, you find that the statements of Canadian International Paper are not available but Powell River are. In so far as the meat industry is concerned, we know all about Canada Packers but we know nothing about Swift Canadian. In so far as the oil industry is concerned, we know about the operations of Imperial Oil, but Cities Service, and a host of others are completely secret. In the merchandising field, the statements of Simpson's are available but Eaton's are not. In so far as farm implements are concerned, if you think you are paying too much for your farm implements, you can ascertain how much Massey-Harris is making, but not International Harvester. In the food industry we find that Weston's operations are open to the public, but General Foods, Nabisco, Heinz and a lot of others are not.
This is an added inducement to foreign companies to refuse to allow Canadians to buy stock in the Canadian subsidiary, because if they allow Canadians to buy stock they will lose the benefit of this quirk in the Companies Act which states that a private company has 50 shareholders or less and a public company is one in which there are more than 50 stockholders. This type of thinking is in line with the former legislation which made it an advantage if a company had 95 per cent or more foreign ownership because if the ownership was of that degree greater tax concessions were received It is a type of thinking that is not colonialism, but it is economic feudalism in my opinion.
As I stated at the outset, there are many points which must be considered with a bill such as this. Undoubtedly, the matter is not covered in the way the Department of Justice for instance, might cover the rectifying of this queer omission in our Companies Act up to the level of national sovereignty, if you like,

to which the United Kingdom brought their act in 1948. However, I do not believe any member on this side of the house can quarrel with the intent of the amendment. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) has repeatedly pointed out in his speeches that this and other steps, such as those mentioned in the report of the royal commission, are necessary in order to improve Canadian-United States relations and to give recognition to the need for making the operation of these companies more Canadian in nature.
About a week ago the minister of northern affairs delivered a speech in the Chateau Laurier and, from the tenor of his remarks, one would have thought he was speaking on this bill. Speeches made in the United States by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) have indicated they believe that measures such as these are necessary and will, in the end, react not only to the benefit of Canada but the other countries involved. It is unfortunate that in every case I must make reference to the United States, but the fact is they are by far the major owner of our industrial complex. This was clearly indicated by the table I read earlier.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I do not see how anyone could quarrel with the intent of this bill. It does not place a liability on any foreign company. It only brings such a company into a position of equality with its more truly Canadian counterpart. It does give to the Canadian people the type of information which is so freely available from the ordinary public companies. As I also stated, this measure does not demand any greater degree of disclosure than is demanded by the United States law.
I do not think there is very much more I can usefully add at this stage, Mr. Speaker. I think that this is simply a companion piece, a sort of trilogy, if you like, because I will have other bills coming forward to take care of some of the other loopholes which I feel should be plugged in order to have this country become a nation in the economic as well as in the political sphere. I have in my hand a pamphlet put out by the Canadian institute of international affairs entitled "Foreign Investment in Canada", by J. M. Smith. He ends up by saying something along these lines, that Canadians have benefited greatly from foreign investment, control notwithstanding, in terms of employment, income and living standards. Yet, as Canadians, we are right to be concerned. Is our economic independence slipping away? At what point, if we are losing our economic independence, will we begin to lose our political independence?
Companies Act

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my support for the principle and purpose of this bill. In doing so I must first of all congratulate the hon. member for his short, somewhat hesitant but most certain step toward C.C.F. policy in this connection.
I support the purpose of the bill as indicated by the explanatory notes and congratulate the hon. member for his most interesting speech when introducing the bill. Personally I think it is wrong in principle that large companies and corporations are allowed to get around the law by incorporating as private companies or being considered as such because they have 50 shareholders or less when it is obvious to most hon. members of this house that it is done in order to conceal an examination of their affairs by the public.
In my opinion the protection of the shareholders and the public interest requires and demands that all proper publicity should be given to the activities of large corporations and companies in Canada. Their activities are usually related to the development of natural resources and the welfare of large numbers of human beings whether they be shareholders or employees of the company concerned. I feel that every proper publicity should be given with respect to their financial position, their profit and loss position, their expansion intentions and questions of that sort. It is for that reason I heartedly endorse the hon. member's efforts in this direction by the introduction of this bill.
However, as the previous speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) said, it is a large step. The Companies Act is a most important and complex act. I believe the matter should receive very careful consideration to make certain that we amend the act to best advantage having in view all the circumstances. Therefore, to that end I would suggest that it would be a good idea and one which should win the approval of the sponsor for this bill to be sent to the appropriate committee of this house where the Secretary of State, officials of the companies branch and representatives from other sections of the community could give evidence and thus enable the committee to ensure that either this bill or a similar piece of legislation does the job intended by the hon. member who has introduced this measure.
Because of the importance of the matter I hope the bill will go to a vote before this private members' hour is concluded and I personally would suggest that someone should move an amendment to the effect that the bill be referred to the appropriate committee.

Mr. Speaker, I, like the two hon. gentlemen who preceded me in this debate, feel that a certain amount of congratulations should be extended to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) for the fine way in which he introduced this measure. Although I cannot concur with everything he has said, in large part I must agree.
I should like first to make some reference to the quotations he cited from the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects. He quoted from pages 393 and 394 which consists of that part of the report dealing with foreign investment in Canada.
What the hon. gentleman says about our requiring some control over foreign investment in Canada is absolutely correct and I believe all those who have participated in this debate concurred in that statement. I should like to read from page 392 of the report of the Gordon Commission:
-we believe the main objectives of Canadians in this matter should be; first, to see a larger share of foreign capital invested in the form of bonds and mortgages, which do not involve control of large sectors of the economy; second, to see that the part of foreign investment which is invested in the resource and manufacturing industries is associated in some degree with Canadian capital and Canadian interests-
In my opinion it is impossible to implement the Gordon recommendations merely by making a slight amendment to the Companies Act. In the first place, there have been no amendments to the act since 1934 notwithstanding the reference in the explanatory notes on the right hand page of the bill as printed.

I know the hon. member mentioned the year 1934 in his opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, but the explanatory notes imply that amendments may have been made since then. The English companies act was revised in 1948 and referring to this in the second paragraph of the explanatory note the hon. member's bill states:
The Canadian act was amended in some respects to follow the 1948 English revision; but this provision was not adopted.
This indicates that the mover of the bill is aware of the English revision of 1948 which probably was justified in that country because, unlike Canada, England does not rely in large part on foreign investment.
I think it would be of some interest to the house if I made reference to the fact that

in both the Canadian and English companies acts the definitions of a private company are identical at the present time. Both acts place restrictions on the right to transfer shares. Both impose a restriction of a total of 50 shareholders and in both acts a company is given no right to request that the public subscribe to its shares.
Mr. Speaker, I have made that statement to bring to the attention of the house that the amendment suggested is not in any way in conflict with the English act; we have identical legislation at the present time. Section 121 of the act is reprinted in the bill which we are discussing today in identical form, with the addition of the folowing words:
-exempted by subsection (2A) -
In other words, if Bill No. C-22 is adopted it will not be making a change in the law in so far as public companies are concerned but it will be making a drastic change in what has been referred to as private companies. In England they have a similar section to section 121. A public company or a private company in England must give 21 days' notice to its shareholders; an English company must also give 21 days' notice to debenture holders. However, we have not that compulsion in Canada.
Personally I have no objection to compelling Canadian private companies to send out their financial statements to their shareholders. There are only 50 shareholders in any case, and in most instances the shareholders are very familiar with the financial statements. In fact, our present act, by section 121 (3), gives the shareholder of a private company, if he is one of the 50, the right to request a financial statement, and it must be mailed to him within a period of seven days. However, there is a small penalty: The shareholder can be obligated to pay 10 cents a folio, or 100 words, for the preparation of the financial report.
As far as I am concerned I have no objection to the bill in so far as a private company being obligated to send out free of charge to its shareholders its financial statement. I have no objection to the statements which have been made by the member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard). However, there is one basic point which I think all of us at all times should be concerned with if we want to keep free enterprise alive in this country of ours. This bill assumes that the internal affairs of a federal private company are of public interest even when there is no questien of this private company going to the public to borrow money or of asking it to subscribe in any way to its security
Companies Ac I
issues.	In my opinion this matter concerns the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian association of chartered accountants.
If we adopted the bill in its present form I suggest we would be creating three types of companies in Canada. In the first place we would be left with the public company, the large company in which anybody can buy shares.	In the second place the private
company, that is the family company which has not more than 50 shareholders, would remain in existence with the same privileges as it has today. The third type of company would be a new creature of fiction. We would be creating a private company which, like the one just mentioned, would not have more than 50 shareholders but it would have to comply with section 121 of the act and the bill we are discussing.
The bill has four conditions, and it is these four conditions I am chiefly concerned with. In the first place the conditions are objectionable because the restrictions or exceptions are cumulative in effect and it would be impractical for anybody to administer the same. The first clause of the bill reads:
(a) No body corporate is the holder of any of the shares or debentures.
Now, if a body corporate became a holder of a share or shares of a private company, that company would then become this new type of company, the third type which I mentioned a moment ago. That could happen very easily in many of the family industries or companies of Canada. It could happen, for example, if a legitimate private company of not more than 50 shareholders went to a bank, borrowed money, and was compelled to put up some of its shares for security. In other words, if a private company went to a bank and the bank insisted on a transfer of shares for security purposes, naturally that company would fall within the ambit of this legislation and would be obligated to comply with section 121. It would then mean that the financial report of that company would be filed in the office of the Secretary of State and the information contained therein would be public in nature, which is certainly contrary to the principe of a private company.
The same thing would happen if any one of the 50 shareholders in a private company registered his shares in a holding company or if he sold them to an incorporated investment dealer for transfer to another person. The same objection which I have just mentioned would be applicable to clauses (b) and (c) which follow.

The last clause (d) is also weak and I suggest, as was also suggested by the hon. member, it is merely a question of bad drafting. However, I feel it should be pointed out, that in Canada today in order to be a director of a Canadian company it is necessary to be an individual, while section (d) says:
no body corporate is a director-
That, I suggest, is merely bad drafting.
What I am also very much concerned about is the objection raised by the hon. member for Ottawa East: Do we know whether or not the Department of the Secretary of State could administer this act if it was adopted in its present form or in some type of amended form? In the first place, it would require a tremendous increase in the staff. The Secretary of State would have to keep a list of all shareholders of every private company and record every individual notice of transfer of shareholdings. He would probably be compelled to hire a large number of inspectors who would be travelling across Canada visiting the head offices of these private companies. I suggest to hon. members that before this bill is passed the Department of the Secretary of State and the solicitors concerned would have to make an exhaustive study and probably introduce a series of amendments in order to make Bill No. C-22 operative.
Personally, I am not at all concerned about requiring private companies to distribute automatically their financial statements to shareholders and to perform this service free of charge. It would not cost them very much. They are obliged to prepare statements by the Companies Act; it would just be a matter of having them mimeographed and distributed.
One point which has not been mentioned is this: because certain things work well in England or in a foreign country this fact alone is no indication that they would work equally well in Canada. I say this because in England, for example, there is just one jurisdiction which can issue letters patent while in Canada there are 11 jurisdictions which have authority to issue letters patent to corporations.
As far as I am concerned, this bill in its present form or in any form which the House of Commons should amend it would always remain ineffective unless we were assured beforehand that all the ten individual authorities would follow suit.
I suggest that before the house votes on this measure it should be studied by the federal-provincial committee which will be meeting again this spring to study the uniformity of Canadian company law. At the
[Mr. Creaghan.l
present time a draft uniform companies act has been prepared. It has been circulated to the various attorneys general, and has been studied by the Canadian Bar Association. I understand that this revised act will be reviewed when this federal-provincial committee meets again some time next month. After study by that committee the measure could possibly be introduced in a better form and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce where delegations could present briefs and the members of the committee could receive the benefit of the expert advice which is available in the capital city.
I wish to emphasize once again that I am in complete accord with the recommendations of the Gordon report. I am opposed to the influx of United States capital into this country in its present form by means of which it can obtain control of the equity stock in new and growing Canadian companies. However, I do not feel that this bill could correct the situation. I believe this matter requires to be dealt with in separate legislation in the form of a bill which would be drafted in such a way as to have some control over the flow of United States or other foreign currency into this country.

For the purpose of completing the record, it might be of interest to read into the record just exactly what a private company is now, as defined by the Companies Act in chapter 53 of the latest edition of the Revised Statutes of Canada. There are three particular matters which help to

define what a private company is. The first, of course, is that the right to transfer its shares is restricted. Second, the number of shareholders is limited to 50 and, third, any invitation to the public to subscribe for any shares or debentures is prohibited. The definition is set forth more explicitly and much more fully in the interpretation section of the act, section 3 (j).
To these factors which now make up a private company, the hon. member has introduced others which are set forth in the second paragraph of Bill No. C-22 now before us for our consideration. I am wondering if he does have in mind the correcting of one ill, where, by the use of hanky-panky and legal ritual, some companies are able to classify themselves as private companies and thus avoid making any disclosure, while other companies are public companies doing the same type of business and must, therefore, make those disclosures. Perhaps he would be better advised even at this stage to consider withdrawing this particular measure and bringing in something which would effect a new definition of what exactly is a private company.
Companies Act
With regard to the other point which, I gather, is concerned with the prevention of United States domination of the Canadian economy, I would say that this bill is really of little use along that line. It would certainly make apparent the extent of the control exercised by United States capital in this country, but it would not change the present situation one bit, and therefore I wonder if the hon. member is really serving the purpose he wishes to serve by means of this bill.
Those are the two reservations I have about this measure. I am afraid that I do not understand it as well as I should. It seems to me that the Companies Act is a difficult field to enter. I hope some brave soul will tackle it one day, refine it, streamline it and even write it in basic English. I appreciate the sincerity of the hon. member, and would be prepared to vote for this bill. However, I see that the hour of the voting has come; perhaps it is now past, and I hope we can achieve in committee the notable objectives which he has in mind.
